Nwosu's analysis suggests another source: in samples from three deserts, the manganese in the varnish occurred in a chemical form that is produced when sunlight reacts with manganese dissolved in dew, a process requiring no biological activity at all.
RW1.stem: According to the text, what did Nwosu's analysis suggest?

Text 2
Critics of the hunting hypothesis note that the extinctions also coincided with abrupt climate change at the end of the last ice age. A recent study, however, examined an island off the coast of Alaska that people did not reach until thousands of years after they reached the mainland. RW2.stem: Based on the texts, how would Akande (Text 1) most likely respond to the study described in Text 2?

She would claim that the study shows people must have reached the island earlier than researchers believe.
She would concede that the study undermines her view, since the island's mammoths died out without any human involvement.

Arctic terns dove more often per hour than any other species at both the strong-current site and the weak-current site.
Common murres dove less often per hour at the strong-current site than at the weak-current site.
At the strong-current site, the two species that feed near the surface dove a combined 55 times per hour.

RW1.passage: A librarian argues that the rise of digital formats at her library has not come at the expense of print. As evidence, she points out that from 2019 to 2023,
RW1.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?
choices: e-book checkouts rose from about 21,000 to about 40,000.
print checkouts fell from about 82,000 to about 64,000 as e-book checkouts rose from about 21,000 to about 38,000.
e-book and audiobook checkouts both increased while print checkouts rose slightly, from about 82,000 to about 84,000.
audiobook checkouts more than doubled, from about 9,000 to about 22,000.
RW1.explain: The claim is about print not suffering while digital grew, so the evidence has to show both: digital up and print holding steady or rising. C does. B is the trap: its numbers are real but come from 2019 to 2021, not 2023, and print falling would undercut the librarian. A and D show digital growth only and say nothing about print.

RW1.passage: Archaeologists have found that many millstones used in Roman Britain were cut from a coarse sandstone quarried in only one region of northern England. Millstones of this stone turn up at sites as far as 300 kilometers from the quarry, including several sites that lie much closer to other stone suitable for grinding grain. This suggests that
RW1.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: most sites in Roman Britain lacked access to any stone suitable for millstones.
the quarry in northern England was the only source of millstones before the Roman period.
millstones made from the coarse sandstone wore out faster than millstones made from other stone.
the sandstone from northern England was valued enough that people transported it long distances even when nearer stone was available.
RW1.explain: People hauled this stone up to 300 km to places that had usable stone nearby. The likeliest reason is that they preferred it. A is contradicted: several sites had suitable stone closer by. B is about an earlier period the text never covers. C would make the long haul less sensible, not more.

RW1.passage: Some birds add aromatic plants such as yarrow to their nests, and researchers have long suspected that the plants keep parasites away. In a study of European starlings, however, nests with added yarrow held just as many mites as nests without it. Even so, chicks raised in the yarrow nests gained weight faster. The researchers concluded that if the plants do benefit chicks,
RW1.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: starlings must add yarrow to their nests in order to raise chicks successfully.
the benefit probably does not come from reducing the number of parasites in the nest.
mites are unlikely to cause any harm to starling chicks.
yarrow probably attracts mites to nests rather than keeping them away.
RW1.explain: Mite numbers were the same with or without yarrow, yet chicks still did better, so whatever helps them isn’t fewer parasites. A overreaches (“must”); chicks in plain nests survived. C draws a conclusion about mites the study didn’t test. D is contradicted by the equal mite counts.

RW1.passage: The Chauvet Cave in southern France, which contains some of the oldest known figurative paintings in Europe,  in 1994 by three cave explorers who felt a faint draft of air coming from a pile of rocks.
RW1.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: discovered
being discovered
was discovered
having been discovered
RW1.explain: Strip the clause between commas and the sentence reads “The Chauvet Cave …  in 1994.” It has no main verb yet, so the blank needs a finite one. Only was discovered is finite and fits “by three cave explorers.” B and D are nonfinite. A is finite only as an active verb (the cave discovered something), which clashes with “by … explorers.”

RW1.passage: Glassblower Ines Moreau begins each piece by gathering molten glass on the end of a long hollow  she blows into the pipe while turning it, shaping the glass with wet wooden paddles.
RW1.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: pipe, after that
pipe after that,
pipe, after that,
pipe; after that,
RW1.explain: Both halves are complete sentences, so they need a semicolon (or a period) between them, and the introductory “after that” takes a comma. A and C join two sentences with only a comma (a comma splice). B has no boundary punctuation at all.

RW1.passage: The collection of more than 300 hand-drawn maps that the cartographer produced during her four decades at the survey office  now housed at the state archive in Olympia.
RW1.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: are
were
have been
is
RW1.explain: The subject is collection (singular); “of more than 300 hand-drawn maps that …” is a long modifier. “Now” calls for present tense: is. A, B, and C are plural verbs that agree with maps, the nearest noun, which is the trap.

RW1.passage: Engineer Amara Diallo’s invention—a pair of gloves fitted with sensors that track finger  translates sign language into synthesized speech.
RW1.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: movement—
movement,
movement;
movement
RW1.explain: The phrase about the gloves interrupts the sentence and opens with a dash, so it must close with a dash. A comma (B) or semicolon (C) can’t close a dash-opened interruption, and D leaves it unclosed, making “movement translates” read as the main clause.

RW1.passage: Entomologist Rui Matsuda recorded the temperature inside forty beehives every hour for an entire winter,  that colonies with more bees kept their cores warmer while eating less honey per bee.
RW1.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: she found
finding
finds
found
RW1.explain: The sentence already has its subject and main verb (Matsuda recorded). After the comma, the blank begins a modifier that describes what the recording showed, so it needs the nonfinite finding. A makes a second complete sentence after a comma (a comma splice). C and D are finite verbs with no subject or conjunction to attach them.

RW1.passage: For the harvest festival, volunteers spent six months sewing the twelve  costumes, each one embroidered with the name of a local farm.
RW1.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: dancers’
dancer’s
dancers
dancers’s
RW1.explain: Twelve costumes belong to twelve dancers, so you need a plural possessive: dancers’. B is singular possessive (one dancer). C is a plain plural with no possession. D isn’t a standard form for a plural ending in s.

RW1.passage: The museum’s new exhibit on the Columbia River brings together three kinds of  woven fishing nets made by Indigenous fishers, survey instruments used to plan the river’s dams, and photographs of towns that the dams’ reservoirs later flooded.
RW1.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: objects;
objects, such as:
objects, which
objects:
RW1.explain: A complete clause (“The exhibit brings together three kinds of objects”) introduces a list, which is the colon’s job. A semicolon (A) must join two complete clauses. “Such as” followed by a colon (B) is redundant and incorrect. “Which” (C) starts a clause that never gets its verb.

RW1.passage: For much of the twentieth century, agronomists advised farmers in the region to plow their fields deeply every fall, burying weed seeds where they could not sprout. Deep plowing, , also exposes soil to wind and rain, and over decades the region’s fields lost much of their topsoil.
RW1.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices: however
therefore
for example
similarly
RW1.explain: The first sentence gives the benefit of deep plowing; the second gives a cost that cuts against it. That’s a contrast: however. “Therefore” wrongly makes erosion the purpose or result of the advice; “for example” and “similarly” don’t fit a downside.

RW1.passage: Most sharks must swim constantly to push water over their gills. The nurse shark, which spends much of its time on the seafloor, can instead pump water over its gills while lying still.  the nurse shark can rest in caves and crevices for hours at a time.
RW1.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices: Nevertheless,
Likewise,
As a result,
By contrast,
RW1.explain: The contrast with other sharks is already made in the second sentence. The blank’s sentence states a consequence of that ability: because it can breathe while still, it can rest for hours. “By contrast” repeats a contrast that’s already been drawn, and there is nothing in the last sentence to contrast with the one before it. “Nevertheless” implies the resting happens despite the gill pumping.

RW1.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • The Bay of Fundy, between New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, has some of the largest tidal ranges in the world.
  • At Burntcoat Head, the difference between high and low tide can reach 16 meters.
  • In the Mediterranean Sea, tidal ranges are typically less than half a meter.
  • The Mediterranean is nearly enclosed, connected to the Atlantic only by the narrow Strait of Gibraltar.
RW1.stem: The student wants to contrast the tidal ranges of the two bodies of water. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: While tidal ranges in the Bay of Fundy can reach 16 meters, those in the Mediterranean Sea are typically less than half a meter.
The Bay of Fundy, between New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, has some of the largest tidal ranges in the world.
The Mediterranean Sea is nearly enclosed, connected to the Atlantic only by the narrow Strait of Gibraltar.
Both the Bay of Fundy and the Mediterranean Sea have tides, although they are in different parts of the world.
RW1.explain: The goal names two things (both bodies of water) and one relationship (contrast in tidal range). A gives both ranges side by side. B covers only Fundy, C only the Mediterranean’s shape, and D gives a similarity (both have tides) wrapped in a contrast word.

RW1.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • Weaver Talia Brenner and potter Joon Park both sold work at the 2024 Skagit Valley craft fair.
  • Brenner dyes her wool with plants she grows herself.
  • Park buys commercially prepared glazes.
  • Both artists sold out on the fair’s first day.
RW1.stem: The student wants to emphasize a difference between the two artists’ materials. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: Although Brenner and Park work in different media, both artists sold out on the fair’s first day.
Brenner dyes her wool with plants she grows herself, whereas Park buys commercially prepared glazes.
Brenner dyes her wool with plants she grows herself, and Park makes pottery.
Brenner and Park, a weaver and a potter, both sold work at the 2024 Skagit Valley craft fair.
RW1.explain: Only B contrasts their materials: homegrown plant dyes vs store-bought glazes. A opens with a contrast word but its actual content is a similarity (both sold out). C names Park’s medium, not her materials. D is a similarity.

RW1.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • Octopuses have about 500 million neurons.
  • Roughly two-thirds of those neurons are in the octopus’s eight arms rather than in its central brain.
  • Researchers have observed severed octopus arms continuing to reach for and grasp food.
  • Neuroscientist Dana Ilunga studies how the arms coordinate with the central brain.
RW1.stem: The student wants to explain why researchers think octopus arms may make some decisions on their own. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: Octopuses have about 500 million neurons, and neuroscientist Dana Ilunga studies them.
Because about two-thirds of an octopus’s neurons are in its arms, and severed arms can still reach for and grasp food, researchers suspect the arms make some decisions independently.
Neuroscientist Dana Ilunga studies how an octopus’s eight arms coordinate with its central brain.
Severed octopus arms have been observed reaching for food, even though most of an octopus’s neurons are in its central brain.
RW1.explain: The goal asks for an explanation (a reason), so the answer needs the two supporting facts: neurons are mostly in the arms, and severed arms still act. B gives both. D flips the second note (two-thirds are in the arms, not the brain). A and C describe the research without giving a reason.

RW2.passage: Historian Lucía Benavides argues that the reputation of the 1890s as an era of unchecked industrial expansion is somewhat : although factory output did grow quickly over the decade, it did so in fits and starts, interrupted by two severe depressions that idled a fifth of the workforce.
RW2.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: overstated
unfounded
obscure
irrefutable
RW2.explain: Benavides grants the growth (“did grow quickly”) but says it wasn’t “unchecked.” The reputation exaggerates: it is somewhat overstated. Unfounded is too strong; it would mean there was no basis at all, yet she concedes the growth happened. Irrefutable reverses her point.

RW2.passage: The poet’s late collections are often described as austere, but the description is  only if one reads them selectively: the poems critics like to quote are indeed spare, yet the books also contain long, digressive pieces crowded with names, recipes, and jokes.
RW2.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: misleading
ambiguous
defensible
novel
RW2.explain: The sentence says the label “austere” holds up only if you read selectively, since the quoted poems are spare but much of the rest isn’t. A label that holds up only under that condition is defensible only that way. Misleading flips the logic: the description isn’t misleading only when read selectively; selective reading is what makes it work.

RW2.passage:
The following text is from a novel. Halvard, a ship’s carpenter, has come home to his village after many years at sea.

The village had not changed so much as . The same houses stood along the same lane, but each seemed to have drawn a little nearer to the ground, and the church spire, which he remembered as reaching nearly to the clouds, now barely cleared the elms.
RW2.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: vanished
expanded
modernized
settled
RW2.explain: The houses are the same but seem to have “drawn … nearer to the ground,” and the spire seems lower: the village appears to have sunk or settled. Expanded and modernized contradict “the same houses … the same lane.” Vanished contradicts the houses still standing.

RW2.passage: Although the witness’s account was, in its broad outlines,  the physical evidence, the attorney pointed to several small discrepancies in timing that the account could not explain.
RW2.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: incompatible with
consistent with
unrelated to
identical to
RW2.explain: “Although” sets up a contrast with the discrepancies, so in broad outline the account must have agreed with the evidence: consistent with. Identical to is too strong for something that has discrepancies. Incompatible with removes the contrast that “although” requires.

RW2.passage: Ecologists have long held that invasive species damage the ecosystems they enter, and in many cases the evidence is overwhelming. <u>Yet a growing number of studies document invasive plants providing food or shelter for native animals, sometimes in places where native plants have already disappeared.</u> Ecologist Maren Sjöberg argues that such findings should not be read as a defense of invasions; rather, they show that removing an invasive species can carry costs that management plans must account for.
RW2.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
choices: It introduces evidence that complicates the view presented in the first sentence.
It provides an example that supports the claim that invasive species damage ecosystems.
It presents the conclusion that Sjöberg reaches about how invasive species should be managed.
It describes the evidence that Sjöberg uses to argue that invasions should be encouraged.
RW2.explain: “Yet” signals a turn: after the long-held view (invasives cause harm), the sentence brings in studies showing invasives sometimes help native animals, which complicates that view. Sjöberg’s conclusion (C) comes in the next sentence. D reverses her position: she says the findings are not a defense of invasions. B gets the direction of the evidence backward.

RW2.passage:
The following text is from a short story. Mrs. Okafor is teaching her grandson to drive.

“Both hands,” she said, though both of his hands were already on the wheel. Desmond nodded. “Mirror,” she said, and he checked it, and she watched him check it, and then she checked it herself. They had not yet left the driveway. In forty years of driving she had never once had an accident, a fact she had mentioned to him four times that morning, and it occurred to her now that perhaps the record was not entirely a matter of skill.
RW2.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the final sentence in the text as a whole?
choices: It reveals that Mrs. Okafor has misled Desmond about her driving record.
It shows that Mrs. Okafor has decided that Desmond is not yet ready to drive.
It explains why Mrs. Okafor has mentioned her driving record so often that morning.
It suggests that Mrs. Okafor is beginning to recognize that her extreme caution may account for her record as much as her skill does.
RW2.explain: The passage piles up her caution (instructions he’s already following, checking the mirror after he does, not yet out of the driveway). The last sentence has her realize the spotless record may owe something to that caution rather than “entirely” to skill. Nothing suggests the record is false (A) or that she has made a decision about Desmond (B). The sentence doesn’t explain her repetition (C); it reflects on the record itself.

RW2.passage:
Text 1
City planners increasingly promote cool roofs, which are coated in white or reflective material. Studies show that such roofs can lower a building’s roof surface temperature by as much as 30°C on a sunny day and reduce air-conditioning use in the rooms beneath, making them an inexpensive tool for coping with summer heat.

Text 2
Climate scientist Ji-ho Baek modeled what would happen if every building in a humid coastal city installed a cool roof. Individual buildings stayed cooler, as expected, but cooler land surfaces across the whole city weakened the afternoon sea breeze, and the model showed less summer rainfall in farmland inland. Baek does not dispute the benefits for single buildings; she argues that before cities mandate cool roofs, their effects at the scale of a whole region need study.
RW2.stem: Based on the texts, how would Baek (Text 2) most likely respond to the planners’ view in Text 1?
choices: By questioning whether cool roofs actually lower surface temperatures as much as the planners claim
By accepting the building-level benefits the planners cite while cautioning that adopting cool roofs across a whole city may have effects those benefits don’t capture
By arguing that cool roofs should be required in humid coastal cities in order to increase inland rainfall
By claiming that the reduction in air-conditioning use matters less than the increase in rainfall in nearby farmland
RW2.explain: Baek “does not dispute the benefits for single buildings” but warns that citywide use can weaken sea breezes and reduce inland rain. That is B. A contradicts her acceptance of the building-level effect. C reverses both her stance (she urges caution before mandates) and the model’s result (less rain). D also gets the rainfall direction wrong.

RW2.passage: Economist Hyun-woo Lim studies why some small towns in the Midwest have kept their populations while neighboring towns have shrunk. Many observers credit local employers: a town with a large factory or hospital, they suggest, will hold on to its residents. Lim’s data complicate that account. Among the towns he studied, those that kept their populations were no more likely than shrinking towns to have a large employer. They were, however, far more likely to lie within a 30-minute drive of a mid-sized city, which let residents keep their homes while commuting to jobs elsewhere.
RW2.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Lim argues that towns with large employers tend to lose population because residents would rather commute.
Lim found that most residents of small Midwestern towns commute to jobs in mid-sized cities.
Lim’s findings suggest that being near a mid-sized city does more than having a large local employer to explain which towns kept their populations.
Lim’s research shows that large local employers are the main reason some towns have kept their populations.
RW2.explain: Lim’s data show that large employers didn’t distinguish growing from shrinking towns, while proximity to a mid-sized city did. D restates the view Lim’s data complicate. A invents a causal claim (employers cause loss). B overgeneralizes from “more likely to lie within a 30-minute drive” to “most residents commute.”

RW2.passage:
The following text is from a novel. Teodora has been asked to speak at her former teacher’s retirement party.

Teodora had written the speech three times. The first version listed Mr. Aldana’s accomplishments, which were many, and she abandoned it halfway through because it read like the back of a book jacket. The second told the story of the afternoon he kept her after class to say that her essay was the worst thing she had ever written and also the most interesting, and she abandoned that one too, because she could not decide whether the story flattered him. The third version was two sentences long. She suspected it was the best of the three, and she was fairly sure she would not have the nerve to read it.
RW2.stem: According to the text, why did Teodora abandon the second version of the speech?
choices: She was unsure whether the story it told would reflect well on Mr. Aldana.
She thought it read too much like a list of accomplishments.
She worried that it was too long to read at the party.
She realized that Mr. Aldana would probably not remember the afternoon it described.
RW2.explain: The second version was dropped “because she could not decide whether the story flattered him,” meaning she couldn’t tell whether it reflected well on him. B is the reason for abandoning the first version. Length (C) is mentioned only for the third, and memory (D) never comes up.

RW2.passage: Paleoclimatologist Ngozi Adeyemi hypothesizes that a prolonged drought around 1200 CE led the residents of a settlement in the American Southwest to abandon it.
RW2.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Adeyemi’s hypothesis?
choices: Tree-ring records from the region show unusually narrow rings, which indicate low rainfall, for the two decades before 1200 CE.
Excavations show that residents of the settlement built new grain-storage rooms during the drought years and continued living there for about forty years after the drought ended.
Several other settlements in the region were also abandoned around 1200 CE.
Pollen samples show that the area around the settlement had fewer drought-tolerant plants before 1200 CE than after it.
RW2.explain: If people stayed through the drought, even expanding food storage, and remained for decades after it ended, the drought can’t explain their leaving. That weakens the hypothesis. A and D are evidence that the drought happened, which supports the hypothesis, as does C (a regional pattern fits a regional drought).

RW2.passage: In a novel, the narrator portrays her brother Matteo as someone who is generous in ways he refuses to acknowledge.
RW2.stem: Which quotation from the novel most effectively illustrates this portrayal?
choices: “Matteo lent money to anyone who asked, and he kept a small notebook in which he recorded every loan to the penny.”
“Matteo was always the first to arrive at family dinners and the last to leave, folding chairs long after everyone else had gone home.”
“When our mother thanked him for driving her to the clinic each week, Matteo said only that he’d been going that way anyway, though the clinic was an hour in the opposite direction from his office.”
“Matteo was not a talkative man, and he seemed to regard conversation as a tax he paid in exchange for being left alone.”
RW2.explain: The portrayal has two parts: generosity, and refusing to acknowledge it. C has both: a weekly two-hour detour for his mother, brushed off with “going that way anyway.” A shows generosity but a careful accounting of it, not a refusal to acknowledge it. B shows helpfulness with no deflection. D shows reserve with no generosity.

in Phoenix, sidewalks under canopies (43°C) were hotter than even the sidewalks in full sun in Seattle (41°C).
in Seattle, sidewalks in full sun (41°C) were 9°C hotter than sidewalks under canopies (32°C).
in Denver, sidewalks in full sun (48°C) were 17°C hotter than the average noon air temperature (31°C).

RW2.passage: A music critic claims that the recent decline in live-music attendance has been concentrated among younger adults.
RW2.stem: Which choice best describes data from the graph that weaken the critic’s claim?
choices: Adults aged 18–29 had the highest attendance rate of any age group in both 2015 and 2023.
Attendance fell in every age group between 2015 and 2023.
Attendance among adults aged 30–44 fell from 52% to 49% between 2015 and 2023.
Attendance among adults aged 18–29 fell from 58% to 55%, a much smaller drop than among adults 60 and older, whose attendance fell from 39% to 27%.
RW2.explain: To weaken “concentrated among younger adults,” show that older adults dropped more. D does: 3 points for 18–29 vs 12 points for 60+. A compares levels, not declines. B says every group fell but not where the drop was concentrated. C shows a younger group declining, which leans toward supporting the critic.

RW2.passage: Many plant species that grow on serpentine soils (soils high in toxic metals and low in nutrients) are found nowhere else. One explanation is that these species thrive only in serpentine chemistry. But when botanist Elena Varga grew several such species in ordinary garden soil, most grew larger than they did on serpentine. When she grew them alongside common grasses in garden soil, however, the serpentine species were quickly crowded out. These results suggest that
RW2.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: the serpentine species are restricted to serpentine soils not because they need its chemistry but because few competitors can survive there.
serpentine soils contain nutrients that the serpentine species need and that garden soil lacks.
common grasses would quickly crowd out the serpentine species on serpentine soils as well.
the serpentine species grow larger on serpentine soil when common grasses are present.
RW2.explain: Alone in garden soil the species do fine, even better; with competitors they lose. So the soil chemistry isn’t what they need; serpentine is where competitors can’t follow. B is contradicted by the better growth in garden soil. C ignores the setup: grasses mostly can’t grow on serpentine. D has no support.

RW2.passage: Historians of medieval Iceland rely heavily on the sagas, which were written down in the thirteenth century but describe events of the tenth and eleventh centuries. Because the sagas include vivid details about farms, feuds, and lawsuits, some historians have treated them as reliable records of the earlier period. Others note that saga writers often described buildings and legal procedures as they existed in the writers’ own time, not in the time they were writing about. If the second group is correct, a historian who used the sagas to reconstruct tenth-century legal procedures would most likely
RW2.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: find that tenth-century procedures were more complex than thirteenth-century ones.
be unable to find any descriptions of legal procedures in the sagas.
produce an account that partly reflects thirteenth-century procedures instead.
conclude that the sagas were written in the tenth century.
RW2.explain: If writers projected their own era’s procedures backward, a tenth-century reconstruction built from the sagas would carry thirteenth-century practice in it. A makes a comparison the text gives no basis for. B contradicts the vivid lawsuit details. D contradicts the stated dates.

RW2.passage: The Polynesian navigators who settled islands scattered across thousands of kilometers of open Pacific, reading ocean swells, stars, and the flight paths of seabirds to find land that lay far beyond the horizon,  some of the most remarkable voyages in human history.
RW2.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: completing
to complete
having completed
completed
RW2.explain: Subject: The Polynesian navigators. Then comes a “who” clause and a long “reading …” phrase, and the sentence still has no main verb. The blank must supply a finite verb: completed. A, B, and C are all nonfinite and would leave the sentence a fragment.

RW2.passage: In 2021 the city restored a creek that had been buried in a concrete pipe beneath a parking lot since the 1950s,  about a kilometer of open water and wetland to the neighborhood.
RW2.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: returned
returns
returning
and it returns
RW2.explain: “The city restored a creek” is complete. The phrase after the comma describes the result of the restoration, so it takes a nonfinite participle: returning. A and B are finite verbs left with no subject after a comma. D is grammatical in form but shifts to present tense for a 2021 event.

RW2.passage: The festival’s three headliners each represent a distinct tradition: Amira Haddad, an oud player from  Tomás Ribeiro, a fado singer from Portugal; and Keola Kahale, a slack-key guitarist from Hawaii.
RW2.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: Lebanon,
Lebanon;
Lebanon:
Lebanon
RW2.explain: Each list item contains its own comma (name, description), so the items are separated by semicolons, as the rest of the list shows (“Portugal; and”). A comma (A) would blur the items together; a colon (C) doesn’t separate list items; no punctuation (D) runs two items together.

RW2.passage: Neither the architect nor the engineers who reviewed her plans  able to explain why the footbridge swayed when crowds crossed it in step.
RW2.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: has been
is
have been
was
RW2.explain: With “neither … nor,” the verb agrees with the nearer subject, the engineers, which is plural: have been. A, B, and D are singular and agree with architect instead.

RW2.passage: The plan’s critics did not object to its  they objected to the speed at which the city intended to carry it out.
RW2.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: cost; rather,
cost, rather
cost, rather,
cost rather,
RW2.explain: Two complete clauses need a semicolon (or period) between them, and the adverb rather that opens the second clause takes a comma after it. B and C are comma splices, and D has no boundary punctuation at all.

RW2.passage: By the time the excavation team reached the lowest layer of the site in 2019, the river  much of the surrounding terrace, carrying away artifacts that earlier surveys had recorded.
RW2.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: had eroded
erodes
will have eroded
is eroding
RW2.explain: “By the time” plus a past event (2019) calls for the past perfect: the erosion was complete before the team arrived. B and D are present tense for a past situation. C projects into the future.

RW2.passage: Volcanologist Haruki  thousands of ash samples from the 2011 eruption, found that the ash particles were unusually sharp-edged.
RW2.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: Endo who has collected
Endo, who has collected
Endo; who has collected
Endo—who has collected
RW2.explain: The clause “who has collected … eruption” is nonessential (the name already identifies him), and it closes with a comma before “found,” so it must open with a comma too. A leaves it unopened. C uses a semicolon, which can’t introduce a dependent clause. D opens with a dash but closes with a comma, which is a mismatch.

RW2.passage: Linguists once assumed that whistled languages, in which speakers convey words by whistling, were simple codes that could carry only a handful of fixed messages. Recordings made in the Canary Islands and in northern Turkey,  show whistlers conveying complete sentences, including sentences their listeners had never heard before.
RW2.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices: for instance,
in other words,
similarly,
however,
RW2.explain: The recordings show full, novel sentences, which contradicts the old assumption of a few fixed messages. The relationship is contrast: however. “For instance” would make the recordings an example of the old assumption. “In other words” would make them a restatement of it.

RW2.passage: The common cuckoo lays its eggs in the nests of other birds, which then raise the cuckoo chicks as their own. Some host species have evolved the ability to recognize and reject cuckoo eggs. Cuckoos,  have evolved eggs that closely mimic the color and pattern of their hosts’ eggs.
RW2.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices: for example,
nevertheless,
in turn,
by contrast,
RW2.explain: Hosts adapted to cuckoos; cuckoos adapted back. That’s a reciprocal response: in turn. “By contrast” sounds right because the subject switches from hosts to cuckoos, but the two adaptations aren’t opposed; one answers the other. “Nevertheless” wrongly suggests mimicry happened despite host rejection rather than because of it.

RW2.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • In 1959, the Soviet probe Luna 3 photographed the far side of the Moon for the first time.
  • Its images were blurry and showed few details.
  • In 2019, China’s Chang’e 4 became the first spacecraft to land on the Moon’s far side.
  • Because the far side never faces Earth, both missions had to work around the lack of a direct radio link: Luna 3 stored its photographs and transmitted them later, and Chang’e 4 relayed its signals through a separate satellite.
RW2.stem: The student wants to emphasize a similarity between the two missions. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: Whereas Luna 3 only photographed the Moon’s far side in 1959, Chang’e 4 landed there in 2019.
Luna 3 stored its photographs to transmit them later, while Chang’e 4 relayed its signals through a separate satellite.
Like Luna 3, which photographed the Moon’s far side for the first time, Chang’e 4 returned blurry images that showed few details.
Both Luna 3 and Chang’e 4 had to find a way to send information to Earth from the side of the Moon that never faces it.
RW2.explain: D states a shared challenge, which is the similarity the last note describes. C opens with “Like,” a similarity word, but its content is wrong: only Luna 3’s images are described as blurry. A and B give differences, B even though it draws on the right note.

RW2.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • Ecologist Farida Haidari studied whether streetlights affect when oak trees leaf out in spring.
  • She compared oaks near streetlights with oaks in dark parks in three cities.
  • Oaks near streetlights leafed out up to a week earlier than oaks in dark parks.
  • Leaves that open earlier are more likely to be damaged by late frosts.
RW2.stem: The student wants to explain a possible consequence of Haidari’s finding. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: Haidari compared oaks near streetlights with oaks in dark parks in three cities to study the timing of leaf-out.
Oaks near streetlights leafed out up to a week earlier than oaks in dark parks, which may leave their new leaves more exposed to late frosts.
Oaks in dark parks leafed out up to a week earlier than oaks near streetlights, which may expose their new leaves to late frosts.
Haidari found that streetlights affect when oak trees leaf out in spring.
RW2.explain: A consequence needs the finding plus what follows from it. B links earlier leaf-out near streetlights to frost risk. C reverses which trees leafed out first. A gives the method, and D gives the finding with no consequence.

RW2.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • Many violinists believe that old Italian violins, such as those made by Stradivari, sound better than new instruments.
  • The wood of a violin changes as it ages.
  • In a blind test, professional violinists could not reliably tell old Italian violins from high-quality new ones.
  • In the same test, the players more often preferred the new violins.
RW2.stem: The student wants to present a finding that challenges a common belief. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: Many violinists believe that old Italian violins sound better than new ones, and the wood of a violin changes as it ages.
Because a violin’s wood changes as it ages, old Italian violins sound better than new ones, a belief many violinists share.
Although many violinists believe that old Italian violins sound better than new ones, blind tests have compared old and new violins.
Despite a common belief that old Italian violins sound better than new ones, professional violinists in a blind test could not reliably tell them apart and more often preferred the new violins.
RW2.explain: D states the belief and then the finding that contradicts it. C has the right contrast word but no finding: “blind tests have compared” says a test happened, not what it showed. B presents the belief as fact and supports it. A just restates the belief.

M1.stem: A jacket’s price is reduced by 30%, and then the sale price is reduced by an additional 10%. The final price is what percent of the original price?
choices: 60%
63%
67%
70%
M1.explain: Multiply the multipliers: 0.70×0.90=0.63, so 63%. Adding the discounts (40% off, giving 60%) is the trap: the second discount applies to a smaller price.

M1.stem: In the figure, line ℓ is parallel to line m, and a transversal crosses both lines. What is the measure, in degrees, of the larger of the two marked angles?
M1.explain: The marked angles are same-side interior angles between parallel lines, so they add to 180∘: (3x+12)+(5x−20)=180, so 8x=188 and x=23.5. The angles are 3(23.5)+12=82.5∘ and 5(23.5)−20=97.5∘. The question asks for the larger angle, not x. Accept 97.5 or 195/2.

M1.stem: A colony of bacteria has 1,500 bacteria at time t=0, and its population increases by 8% every 30 minutes. Which function gives the number of bacteria P(t) after t hours?
choices: P(t)=1,500(1.08)t/2
P(t)=1,500(1.08)2t
P(t)=1,500(1.16)t
P(t)=1,500(0.08)2t
M1.explain: There are two 30-minute periods per hour, so after t hours the 8% growth has applied 2t times: 1,500(1.08)2t. Choice A applies it only once every 2 hours. Choice C adds the rates instead of compounding them (1.082=1.1664, not 1.16).

M1.stem: 2x+3y=21x−y=−2If (x,y) is the solution to the system of equations, what is the value of x+y?
M1.explain: From the second equation, x=y−2. Substituting: 2(y−2)+3y=21, so 5y=25 and y=5; then x=3. The question asks for x+y=8.

M1.stem: A data set consists of the values 12, 15, 15, 18, 20, 23, and 40. If the value 40 is removed, which statement about the mean and median of the data set is true?
choices: The mean decreases, and the median is unchanged.
Both the mean and the median are unchanged.
Both the mean and the median decrease.
The mean is unchanged, and the median decreases.
M1.explain: Mean: 143/7≈20.4 becomes 103/6≈17.2. Median: the middle of 7 values is 18; the middle of the remaining 6 is (15+18)/2=16.5. Both drop. The common trap (A) assumes removing an outlier never moves the median, but removing any value from one end shifts the middle position.

M1.stem: What is the positive difference between the two solutions of x2−10x+21=0?
M1.explain: x2−10x+21=(x−3)(x−7), so the solutions are 3 and 7, which differ by 4.

M1.stem: A delivery van can carry at most 1,200 pounds, including the driver. The driver weighs 180 pounds, and each box weighs 35 pounds. What is the greatest number of boxes the van can carry?
choices: 29
28
30
34
M1.explain: 180+35b≤1,200 gives b≤351,020​≈29.1, so the most whole boxes is 29. Rounding up to 30 breaks the limit. Choice D ignores the driver (1,200/35≈34.3).

M1.stem: What is the radius of the circle in the xy-plane with equation x2+y2−6x+8y=0?

M1.stem: A printer prints 18 pages per minute. At this rate, how many seconds does it take to print 45 pages?
M1.explain: 45÷18=2.5 minutes, and 2.5×60=150 seconds. Stopping at 2.5 answers in the wrong unit.

M1.stem: The functions f and g are defined by f(x)=2x2−3x and g(x)=x−4. What is the value of f(g(−1))?

M1.stem: At a museum, adult tickets cost $12 and child tickets cost $8. A group bought three times as many child tickets as adult tickets and spent a total of $432. How many child tickets did the group buy?
choices: 36
12
24
48
M1.explain: Let a be the number of adult tickets. Then 12a+8(3a)=36a=432, so a=12, and there are 3(12)=36 child tickets. Choice B is the number of adult tickets.

M1.stem: Which expression is equivalent to (3x−2)2−(x+4)(x−4)?

8x2−12x+20
10x2−12x+20

M1.stem: Triangle ABC is similar to triangle DEF, and side AB corresponds to side DE. If AB=6, DE=15, and the area of triangle ABC is 24, what is the area of triangle DEF?
M1.explain: The scale factor is 15/6=2.5, and areas scale by the square: 24×2.52=24×6.25=150. Multiplying by 2.5 gives 60, which scales the area like a length.

M1.stem: In the equation x2+kx+49=0, k is a positive constant. If the equation has exactly one real solution, what is the value of k?
M1.explain: Exactly one real solution means the discriminant is zero: k2−4(1)(49)=0, so k2=196 and k=14 (positive).

M1.stem: The function f is defined by f(x)=a(x−2)(x+6), where a is a constant. In the xy-plane, the graph of y=f(x) has a minimum value of −32. What is the value of a?

M2.stem: A car travels 680 kilometers. The car’s fuel efficiency is 34 miles per gallon, and gasoline costs $3.40 per gallon. What is the cost, in dollars, of the gasoline used for the trip? (Use 1 mile =1.6 kilometers.)
M2.explain: 680÷1.6=425 miles; 425÷34=12.5 gallons; 12.5×3.40=$42.50. Choice D is the number of gallons, not dollars. B skips the unit conversion, and C converts in the wrong direction.

M2.stem: The polynomial p(x)=2x3−5x2+kx−6, where k is a constant, leaves a remainder of 4 when divided by x−2. What is the value of p(−1)?

M2.stem: A caterer charges a flat fee plus a fixed amount per guest. The total charge is $1,180 for 40 guests and $1,705 for 65 guests. What is the caterer’s flat fee, in dollars?

M2.stem: A cylindrical tank with radius 3 feet and height 10 feet is filled with water to 80% of its capacity. All of the water is poured into an empty rectangular tank whose base measures 6 feet by 4 feet. How deep, in feet, is the water in the rectangular tank?

M2.stem: The function f(t)=800(1.21)t models a quantity t years after it was first measured. Which equivalent form of f(t) shows, as a constant or coefficient, the percent increase in the quantity every half-year?

f(t)=800(1.1)2t
f(t)=800(1.21)t/2
f(t)=800(1.4641)t/2

Choice D is also equivalent (1.4641t/2=1.21t), but it shows the two-year factor. Choice A halves the rate instead of taking a square root, and C isn’t equivalent.

M2.stem: In the equation a(2x+3)−4x=6x+b, a and b are constants. If the equation has infinitely many solutions, what is the value of a+b?
M2.explain: Expand: (2a−4)x+3a=6x+b. Infinitely many solutions requires matching coefficients and constants: 2a−4=6 gives a=5, and b=3a=15. So a+b=20.

M2.stem: A random sample of 400 households was selected from a city with 52,000 households. In the sample, 38% of households had solar panels. Based on the sample, the margin of error for the percent of all households in the city with solar panels is 4.6 percentage points. Which of the following is the most plausible number of households in the city that have solar panels?

15,000
20,500
24,000
M2.explain: The plausible range is 38%±4.6%, or 33.4% to 42.6% of 52,000: about 17,370 to 22,150 households. Only 20,500 is in that range. Choice A is 38% of the sample; B and D fall outside the margin.

M2.stem: In the xy-plane, the graphs of y=x2−4x+c and y=2x−3, where c is a constant, intersect at exactly one point. What is the value of c?
M2.explain: Set equal: x2−4x+c=2x−3, so x2−6x+(c+3)=0. One intersection means a zero discriminant: 36−4(c+3)=0, so c+3=9 and c=6.

M2.stem: In triangle XYZ, angle Y is a right angle and cosX=0.6. Point W lies on side XZ so that YW is perpendicular to XZ. What is the value of cos(∠XYW)?

M2.stem: The graph of y=f(x) in the xy-plane passes through the point (2,5). The function g is defined by g(x)=3f(x−4)−1. Which point must lie on the graph of y=g(x)?

M2.stem: The price of a stock increased by 25% on Monday and then decreased by p% on Tuesday. At the end of Tuesday, the price was 10% lower than it was at the start of Monday. What is the value of p?
M2.explain: 1.25(1−100p​)=0.90, so 1−100p​=0.72 and p=28. The tempting 35 (that is, 25+10) treats percents as if they added.

M2.stem: In the xy-plane, the circle with equation (x−4)2+(y+1)2=25 intersects the x-axis at two points. What is the distance between these two points?

M2.stem: For how many integer values of x is (x−2)(x+1)2(x−5)≤0?
M2.explain: Since (x+1)2≥0, the sign depends on (x−2)(x−5), which is ≤0 for 2≤x≤5: the integers 2,3,4,5. The squared factor adds one more: at x=−1 the product equals 0, which satisfies ≤. Total: 5.

M2.stem: Pipe A alone can fill a tank in 6 hours. Pipes A and B working together can fill the tank in 4 hours. How many hours would it take pipe B alone to fill the tank?

M2.stem: The function f is defined by f(x)=ax2+bx+c. The graph of y=f(x) in the xy-plane passes through the points (0,6) and (2,6), and the minimum value of f is −2. What is the value of f(5)?
M2.explain: Points with equal y-values at x=0 and x=2 put the axis of symmetry at x=1, so f(x)=a(x−1)2−2. From f(0)=a−2=6, a=8. Then f(5)=8(16)−2=126.

RW1.passage: Because the comet had been observed for only nine nights, astronomer Ravi Menon described his estimate of its orbital period as : further observations, he noted, could shift the figure by several decades in either direction.
RW1.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: arbitrary
definitive
provisional
redundant
RW1.explain: The colon explains the description: more data could move the estimate by decades, so it is a working figure subject to change, provisional. Definitive is the opposite. Arbitrary goes too far: the estimate rests on nine nights of real observations.

RW1.passage: The architect’s renovation of the 1920s library was notably : rather than replacing the original oak shelving and plaster ceilings, she repaired them, adding new wiring and lighting only where it could be hidden from view.
RW1.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: radical
unobtrusive
extravagant
hasty
RW1.explain: She kept the original features and hid the new work, so the renovation doesn’t call attention to itself: unobtrusive. Radical is the opposite of repairing what was there. Nothing addresses cost (extravagant) or speed (hasty).

RW1.passage:
The following text is from a novel. Ines is watching her grandmother shop at the market.

Abuela moved through the stalls slowly, lifting a tomato here, a melon there, and setting each one down again as if weighing testimony. The vendors, who knew her, did not hurry her. They had learned that her verdicts, once delivered, were final, and that a tomato she approved would soon be bought by half the women watching.
RW1.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “delivered” most nearly mean?
choices: transported
rescued
surrendered
pronounced
RW1.explain: The courtroom language (“weighing testimony,” “verdicts”) sets up the meaning: a verdict that has been delivered has been announced, or pronounced. Transported is the everyday sense (delivering goods), which a market setting makes tempting, but verdicts aren’t carried anywhere.

RW1.passage: Although the 1820 treaty was hailed at the time as a lasting settlement, historian Claire Dubois argues that it was in fact : within a decade, both signatories had violated its central provisions, and the border it drew had been redrawn twice.
RW1.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: ephemeral
unanimous
clandestine
comprehensive
RW1.explain: “Although … lasting” sets up the opposite: the treaty broke down within ten years, so its effect was short-lived, ephemeral. Comprehensive (covering everything) doesn’t contrast with “lasting.” Nothing suggests secrecy (clandestine) or a vote (unanimous).

RW1.passage: Archaeologists studying a Viking ship found in a Danish fjord compared the growth rings in its oak planks with tree-ring records from across northern Europe. The pattern of the rings matched records from forests near Dublin, and the outermost rings showed that the trees had been felled around 1042. The researchers concluded that the ship was built in Ireland and later sailed, or was taken, across the North Sea to Denmark.
RW1.stem: Which choice best describes the main purpose of the text?
choices: To argue that tree-ring dating is more reliable than other methods of dating wooden objects
To explain how researchers determined where and when a ship was built
To describe the trade routes that connected Ireland and Denmark in the eleventh century
To compare the shipbuilding techniques used in two regions of northern Europe
RW1.explain: Each sentence moves toward one result: the rings revealed both the place (Dublin) and the date (about 1042). A would need a comparison with other methods, which the text never makes. C and D bring in topics (trade routes, building techniques) the text doesn’t discuss.

RW1.passage:
The following text is from a novel. Mateo has just started working at a hardware store.

On his first morning, Mateo was handed a broom, a clipboard, and a printed list of the store’s four thousand items. By noon he had learned where the hinges were kept, and that the brass ones sold faster than the steel. By the end of the week, customers had begun asking for him by name, though he still could not have said where the store kept its rope.
RW1.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
choices: It shows Mateo beginning to learn details about the store that go beyond the list he was given.
It suggests that Mateo is frustrated by how much he has to learn about the store.
It explains why customers began asking for Mateo by name.
It reveals that brass hinges are the store’s best-selling item.
RW1.explain: The list names items; the underlined sentence adds knowledge no list contains (which hinges actually sell), the start of Mateo’s real expertise. C is the trap: the customers come up only in the next sentence, and the text never says why they ask for him. D overreads “faster than the steel” into “best-selling item.” Nothing shows frustration (B).

RW1.passage:
Text 1
Some critics worry that emoji are eroding young people’s writing. If a heart or a laughing face can stand in for a sentence, they argue, writers will lose the habit of putting their feelings into words.

Text 2
Linguist Hannah Moreau analyzed thousands of text messages and found that emoji rarely replaced words. Instead, they usually appeared alongside complete sentences, signaling tone (irony, warmth, a joke), much as facial expressions and gestures accompany speech. Messages that contained emoji were, on average, no shorter than messages without them.
RW1.stem: Based on the texts, how would Moreau (Text 2) most likely respond to the critics’ concern in Text 1?
choices: By agreeing that emoji have made text messages shorter but arguing that this change is harmless
By arguing that emoji express feelings more effectively than words do
By suggesting that the critics have underestimated how often emoji replace words
By pointing out that the concern assumes emoji substitute for written words, when her findings suggest they mostly accompany words
RW1.explain: The critics’ worry depends on emoji standing in for sentences. Moreau found the opposite: emoji mostly sit beside full sentences, and messages with emoji were no shorter. A contradicts that length finding. C reverses her result. B makes a claim about effectiveness she never makes.

RW1.passage:
The following text is from a short story. Farida has come back to her hometown after ten years away.

The bakery on the corner had become a phone store, and the river path she had once walked to school was now paved and lit. Farida found she did not mind. What unsettled her was the hardware store, which had not changed at all: the same faded sign, the same cat asleep in the window (though surely not the same cat). It was as if the town had saved one thing exactly as she had left it, and she could not decide whether that was a kindness or a reproach.
RW1.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Farida is less troubled by the changes in her hometown than by the one place that has stayed the same.
Farida is upset that the bakery she remembers has been replaced by a phone store.
Farida regrets having left her hometown ten years earlier.
Farida is pleased to see that her hometown has been modernized.
RW1.explain: Farida “did not mind” the changes; what “unsettled her” was the unchanged hardware store. B contradicts “did not mind.” D overstates it: not minding isn’t the same as being pleased. C may be hinted by “reproach,” but she can’t even decide that, so regret isn’t the main idea.

RW1.passage: Coffee plants produce caffeine in their leaves and seeds, where it deters many plant-eating insects. Ecologist Mira Halvorsen found that the nectar of some coffee flowers also contains caffeine, though at doses far too low to taste bitter. In her experiments, honeybees that fed on caffeinated nectar were three times as likely as bees fed plain sugar water to remember the flower’s scent a day later.
RW1.stem: According to the text, how did caffeinated nectar affect honeybees in Halvorsen’s experiments?
choices: It made them more likely to remember a flower’s scent a day later.
It made them more likely to avoid coffee flowers.
It made them feed on nectar more quickly.
It deterred them from feeding on the leaves of coffee plants.
RW1.explain: The last sentence states the effect: bees on caffeinated nectar were three times as likely to remember the scent a day later. D mixes up two parts of the text: deterrence applies to insects eating leaves, not to bees drinking nectar. B and C aren’t stated.

RW1.passage: Anthropologist Nadia Sami claims that in the fishing villages she studied, older residents’ knowledge of the reef was passed on mainly through shared work rather than through formal instruction.
RW1.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Sami’s claim?
choices: Older residents could name more reef species than younger residents could.
Most villagers said in interviews that they valued the reef and wanted to protect it.
Villagers who had fished alongside older relatives could name more reef species than villagers who had completed a school course on reef ecology.
The village school began offering a course on reef ecology in 2005.
RW1.explain: The claim compares two routes for passing on knowledge (shared work vs formal instruction), so support has to compare them. C does: fishing with elders beat the school course. A shows older residents know more, but not how knowledge moves to the young. B and D don’t bear on how knowledge is transmitted.

RW1.passage: In a novel, the narrator describes her new city as both exhilarating and exhausting.
RW1.stem: Which quotation from the novel most effectively illustrates the claim?
choices: “I had rented a room above a laundromat, and the warm smell of detergent drifted up through the floorboards all night.”
“My mother called every Sunday to ask whether I was eating enough, and every Sunday I told her that I was.”
“On my first morning I bought a map and folded it so many times that the creases wore through the river.”
“The subway roared beneath the street every four minutes, and every four minutes I felt the city had something urgent to tell me, though by evening I could barely keep my eyes open to hear it.”
RW1.explain: The claim has two halves. D gives both: the city seems to have “something urgent to tell” her (exhilarating), and by evening she can hardly stay awake (exhausting). C suggests eager exploration but no exhaustion; A and B describe daily details with neither feeling.

RW1.passage: Ecologist Sun-hee Park surveyed native bee species at four green spaces in one city. She argues that even very small green spaces can support many native bee species, provided that most of their plants are native.
RW1.stem: Which choice best describes data from the table that support Park’s argument?
choices: The cemetery, the largest site at 12.0 hectares, supported 17 native bee species.
The lawn park had the lowest percentage of native plants and the fewest native bee species.
The pocket prairie, the smallest site at 0.2 hectares, had the highest percentage of native plants and the most native bee species.
The community garden supported more native bee species than the lawn park did.
RW1.figure:

SiteArea (hectares)Native plants (%)Native bee species
Community garden0.47231
Lawn park6.089
Pocket prairie0.29534
