RW1.explain: Park’s argument has two conditions (small and mostly native) and a result (many species). The pocket prairie meets both conditions and has the most species. B is accurate, but the lawn park is large, so it says nothing about small spaces. D compares two sites without mentioning size or native plants.

RW1.passage: A city planner notes that the drop in bus commuting in 2020 proved temporary, while the rise in bike commuting lasted:
RW1.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?
choices: bus commuting fell from 21% of commuters in 2015 to 12% in 2020 but recovered to 20% by 2025, while bike commuting rose from 5% to 8% and was still 7% in 2025.
bike commuting fell from 8% of commuters in 2020 to 7% in 2025.
bus commuting rose from 18% of commuters in 2010 to 20% in 2025.
in every year shown, a larger percentage of commuters took the bus than rode a bike.
RW1.explain: The statement makes two claims: the bus drop was temporary, and the bike rise held. A covers both (bus 21 → 12 → 20; bike 5 → 8, still 7). B is true but, alone, points the wrong way: it shows bike commuting slipping. C skips the 2020 drop entirely, and D compares the modes rather than their changes.

RW1.passage: Many medieval European world maps distort distances wildly, place Jerusalem at their center, and fill their margins with scenes from scripture and legend. Such maps were often displayed on the walls of cathedrals rather than carried by travelers. These features suggest that
RW1.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: medieval travelers relied mainly on maps that placed Jerusalem at their center.
the maps were probably meant mainly to convey religious and historical ideas rather than to help people find their way.
medieval mapmakers did not know the actual distances between major cities.
cathedrals were the only places where medieval people could see maps.
RW1.explain: Distorted distances, a symbolic center, scriptural scenes, and display on cathedral walls all point away from practical navigation and toward teaching. A contradicts “rather than carried by travelers.” C and D overreach: the distortion could be deliberate, and nothing says cathedrals were the only place maps were seen.

RW1.passage: The wood frog can survive the freezing of up to two-thirds of the water in its body. As it begins to freeze, its liver releases large amounts of glucose into its blood, which limits the formation of ice inside its cells. Researchers found that wood frogs from Alaska, where winters are long and severe, built up considerably more glucose than wood frogs from Ohio. This finding suggests that
RW1.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: wood frogs from Ohio cannot survive being frozen.
glucose is the only substance that protects wood frogs from freezing.
wood frogs in Alaska freeze more often than wood frogs in Ohio do.
the amount of glucose a wood frog builds up may be related to the severity of the winters it typically experiences.
RW1.explain: Frogs from the harsher climate built up more glucose, so glucose levels may track winter severity. A goes too far (less glucose isn’t none). B overreaches with “only.” C claims a frequency of freezing that the text never measures.

RW1.passage: The Hōkūle‘a, a replica of a traditional Polynesian voyaging canoe that  from Hawaii to Tahiti in 1976 using no modern instruments, has since sailed around the world.
RW1.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: sailing
to sail
sailed
having sailed
RW1.explain: The blank is the verb of the relative clause “that  from Hawaii to Tahiti,” and a relative clause needs its own finite verb: sailed. The sentence’s main verb (“has since sailed”) comes later, after the interrupting phrase. A, B, and D are nonfinite.

RW1.passage: Few musical instruments are older than the  fragments of flutes carved from bird bone and mammoth ivory, found in caves in southern Germany, are more than 35,000 years old.
RW1.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: flute:
flute,
flute
flute, which
RW1.explain: The first clause makes a claim, and the second is the evidence for it. A colon introduces an explanation after a complete clause. B creates a comma splice, C runs the clauses together, and D attaches “which” to a clause that already has its own subject.

RW1.passage: Among the objects recovered from the sixteenth-century wreck  a bronze astrolabe, its scale still legible after nearly five centuries underwater.
RW1.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: were
are
have been
was
RW1.explain: This sentence is inverted: the subject comes after the verb. Ask what was recovered: “a bronze astrolabe,” singular, so the verb is was (past tense for a past recovery). “Objects” sits in the opening prepositional phrase and isn’t the subject.

RW1.passage: When the city’s two oldest libraries merged in 1998,  combined collection became the largest in the state.
RW1.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: its
their
it’s
they’re
RW1.explain: The possessive refers to the two libraries, which are plural: their. A is singular. C and D are contractions (“it is,” “they are”), not possessives.

RW1.passage: To estimate how much water a forest returns to the air, hydrologists sometimes seal plastic bags around individual branches,  the water vapor that the leaves release over the course of a day.
RW1.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: collect
they collect
collecting
collected
RW1.explain: The sentence already has its main clause (“hydrologists … seal plastic bags”). The phrase after the comma explains what the bags do, so it takes the nonfinite collecting. B is a comma splice; A and D are finite verbs with nothing to attach them to.

RW1.passage: Several of the region’s  camas and bitterroot, were staple foods for the Indigenous peoples of the Columbia Plateau.
RW1.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: plants such as
plants, such as
plants; such as
plants: such as
RW1.explain: “Such as camas and bitterroot” is a nonessential example phrase, and it closes with a comma after “bitterroot.” It needs an opening comma to match. A leaves it unopened. C and D use punctuation that can’t introduce a phrase in the middle of a clause.

RW1.passage: Built for the 1889 World’s Fair in Paris,
RW1.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: Gustave Eiffel’s company designed the iron tower to stand for only twenty years.
many Parisians at first considered the iron tower an eyesore.
the iron tower was originally meant to stand for only twenty years.
twenty years was the length of time the iron tower was originally meant to stand.
RW1.explain: The opening phrase describes something that was built, so the word right after the comma must name it: the iron tower. A makes Eiffel’s company the thing built, B makes Parisians the thing built, and D makes “twenty years” the thing built.

RW1.passage: Workers in ancient Egypt moved enormous stone blocks on wooden sledges. Dragging a heavy sledge across dry desert sand is difficult, because the sand heaps up in front of the runners. Wet sand,  is stiffer, and experiments have shown that the right amount of water can cut the force needed to pull a sledge roughly in half.
RW1.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices: similarly,
by contrast,
for instance,
as a result,
RW1.explain: Dry sand heaps up; wet sand is stiffer and lets the sledge slide. The sentence sets the two against each other: by contrast. “Similarly” implies the two kinds of sand behave alike. “As a result” implies wetness follows from the heaping.

RW1.passage: Many people picture the Sahara as a desert that has always looked the way it does today.  satellite images reveal the beds of ancient rivers beneath its sands, and rock paintings in southern Algeria show giraffes and hippopotamuses.
RW1.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices: Thus,
Similarly,
Moreover,
Yet
RW1.explain: The evidence (old riverbeds, paintings of water-loving animals) contradicts the common picture in the first sentence, so the transition is a contrast: yet. “Moreover” and “similarly” would add to or extend the first sentence instead. “Thus” would make the evidence follow from people’s assumption.

RW1.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • The Rosetta Stone is a granite slab found in 1799 near the Egyptian town of Rashid.
  • It carries the same decree written in three scripts: hieroglyphic, Demotic, and ancient Greek.
  • Scholars of the time could read ancient Greek.
  • Jean-François Champollion announced his decipherment of hieroglyphs in 1822.
RW1.stem: The student wants to explain why the Rosetta Stone was useful to scholars trying to read hieroglyphs. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: The Rosetta Stone, a granite slab, was found in 1799 near the Egyptian town of Rashid.
Jean-François Champollion announced his decipherment of hieroglyphs in 1822.
Because the Rosetta Stone carries the same decree in hieroglyphic, Demotic, and Greek, scholars who could read the Greek had a key to the hieroglyphs.
The Rosetta Stone carries writing in three scripts, one of which is Demotic.
RW1.explain: “Why useful” calls for the reason: the same text appears in a script scholars could read. C states it. A and B give dates, and D names the scripts without saying why that mattered.

RW1.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • Emperor penguins and Adélie penguins both live in Antarctica.
  • Emperor penguins breed during the Antarctic winter, on sea ice.
  • Adélie penguins breed during the Antarctic summer, on rocky, ice-free ground.
  • Both species feed mainly on krill and fish.
RW1.stem: The student wants to contrast the two species’ breeding seasons. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: Unlike Adélie penguins, emperor penguins feed mainly on krill and fish.
Emperor penguins breed during the Antarctic winter, whereas Adélie penguins breed during the summer.
Both emperor penguins and Adélie penguins live in Antarctica, though emperors breed on sea ice.
Adélie penguins breed on rocky, ice-free ground during the Antarctic summer.
RW1.explain: B contrasts the seasons directly. A uses a contrast word (“unlike”) to introduce something both species share. C contrasts breeding location, not season. D gives only one species.

RW1.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • Psychologist Ana Lucero studied whether taking notes by hand or on a laptop affects how well students understand lectures.
  • Students who typed tended to record lectures nearly word for word.
  • Students who wrote by hand summarized more, in their own words.
  • On questions requiring conceptual understanding, the handwriting group scored higher.
RW1.stem: The student wants to suggest a possible reason for the difference in scores. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: Lucero studied whether taking notes by hand or on a laptop affects how well students understand lectures.
Students who typed recorded lectures nearly word for word, which may explain why they scored higher on conceptual questions.
On questions requiring conceptual understanding, students who wrote notes by hand scored higher than students who typed.
Students who wrote by hand summarized more in their own words, which may explain why they scored higher on conceptual questions than students who typed.
RW1.explain: A reason needs a cause linked to the result: summarizing in their own words → better conceptual scores. B flips which group scored higher. C gives the result without a reason, and A gives only the study’s question.

RW2.passage: Critics who call the novelist’s late style  misread her intent: the abrupt shifts in tone that seem careless on a first reading turn out, on rereading, to be carefully placed echoes of earlier chapters.
RW2.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: meticulous
haphazard
derivative
sentimental
RW2.explain: The blank is the critics’ label, which the text says is a misreading. What do the critics see? Shifts that “seem careless”: haphazard. Meticulous is the writer’s actual method, the view the text defends, not the critics’ view. Careful reading of whose word it is decides this one.

RW2.passage: Although the ecologist’s new estimate of the region’s wolf population is 15 percent higher than earlier figures, her model does not so much  those figures as refine them: it starts from the same aerial counts and corrects only for animals that forest cover hid from view.
RW2.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: overturn
replicate
inflate
publicize
RW2.explain: “Although … 15 percent higher” raises the expectation that the model rejects the old figures. “Not so much X as refine” denies that expectation, so X is the stronger move: overturn. Replicate doesn’t fit a result that differs by 15 percent, and inflate implies distortion, which the careful correction contradicts.

RW2.passage:
The following text is from a novel. Corinne, a botanist, is cataloging plants on a remote island.

Corinne had expected the island’s plant life to be meager, and in one sense it was: a hundred-odd species, most of them familiar. But the familiar plants had grown strange. The dandelions stood knee-high; the clover had abandoned its creeping habit and climbed. Isolation, she wrote that evening, had not  the island’s plants so much as given them license.
RW2.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: protected
multiplied
disguised
diminished
RW2.explain: Corinne expected meagerness, and the species count was low, but the plants themselves grew larger and bolder. Isolation didn’t shrink them; it freed them: not diminished but “given license.” Multiplied contradicts “a hundred-odd species.” Protected doesn’t contrast with license the way the sentence requires.

RW2.passage: Economist Mariam Diallo’s account of the 1970s inflation is notably : rather than blaming rising oil prices alone, as many accounts do, she assigns responsibility to several causes at once and weighs each against the others.
RW2.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: partisan
cursory
multifaceted
derivative
RW2.explain: Several causes, each weighed against the others, describe an account with many sides: multifaceted. Cursory (hasty, shallow) contradicts the careful weighing. Nothing suggests bias (partisan) or copying (derivative); she departs from “many accounts.”

RW2.passage: For decades, researchers gauged problem-solving in wild birds largely by testing whether the birds could open puzzle boxes to reach food. <u>Such tests favor species that are curious about new objects, and many birds avoid unfamiliar things altogether.</u> Behavioral ecologist Lena Okafor therefore built tasks from materials the birds already handled in the wild, such as bark, moss, and seed pods.
RW2.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
choices: It identifies a limitation of an established method that motivates the approach described next.
It presents evidence that wild birds are less capable problem solvers than researchers once thought.
It explains why Okafor’s tasks were more difficult than earlier puzzle-box tests.
It describes a finding from Okafor’s research on wild birds.
RW2.explain: The sentence points out a flaw in puzzle-box tests (they penalize birds wary of new objects), and “therefore” shows Okafor’s familiar-material tasks respond to it. It doesn’t report a result (B, D), and nothing compares difficulty (C).

RW2.passage: Accounts of the 1890s bicycle craze often emphasize its social effects, especially the freedom it gave women to travel without escorts. Historian Tomás Reyes does not dispute those effects, but he argues that the craze’s most lasting legacy was technical: the demand for bicycles drove improvements in ball bearings, steel tubing, and air-filled tires that the first automobile makers later adopted.
RW2.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
choices: It presents a historian’s claim and then offers evidence that contradicts it.
It describes a technical innovation and then explains its social effects.
It summarizes a debate between two historians and concludes that neither is correct.
It notes a common emphasis in accounts of a historical development, then presents a historian’s argument that a different consequence was more enduring.
RW2.explain: First sentence: the usual emphasis (social effects). Second: Reyes, who accepts those effects, argues the technical legacy lasted longer. B reverses the order and the focus. A misreads Reyes’s “does not dispute” as a contradiction, and C invents a second historian.

RW2.passage:
Text 1
Geneticist Erik Holm argues that dogs were domesticated twice, once in eastern and once in western Eurasia. His evidence is ancient DNA: dog remains older than about 10,000 years fall into two distinct genetic lineages, one found mostly in the east and one mostly in the west.

Text 2
The existence of two ancient dog lineages is well established. But as zooarchaeologist Priya Natarajan notes, the same pattern would arise if dogs were domesticated once and then, as they spread, interbred extensively with different local wolf populations. With the evidence now available, Natarajan argues, the two scenarios cannot be told apart.
RW2.stem: Based on the texts, how would Natarajan (Text 2) most likely respond to Holm’s argument (Text 1)?
choices: By denying that ancient dog remains fall into two distinct genetic lineages
By accepting that the two lineages exist but questioning whether they show that domestication happened twice
By arguing that dogs were most likely domesticated in western Eurasia
By claiming that interbreeding with wolves explains the two lineages better than two domestications do
RW2.explain: Natarajan calls the two lineages “well established” but says one domestication plus interbreeding would produce the same pattern, so the data can’t decide. That’s B. A contradicts her acceptance of the lineages. D is the subtle trap: she says the two scenarios cannot be told apart, not that hers is better.

RW2.passage: Coral reefs depend on algae that live inside coral tissue. When water grows too warm, corals expel the algae and turn white, which is called bleaching. Marine biologist Hana Kaleo found that during a severe heat wave in 2019, corals on reefs that had experienced moderate heat waves in earlier years bleached less than corals on reefs with no such history. Kaleo cautions, however, that this apparent “heat memory” appeared only after moderate events: corals on reefs that had previously suffered severe bleaching were, if anything, more vulnerable.
RW2.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Kaleo’s research suggests that earlier exposure to moderate heat may help corals withstand later heat waves, though earlier severe bleaching does not appear to have the same effect.
Kaleo’s research shows that any past exposure to heat makes corals more resistant to bleaching.
Kaleo found that corals that survive severe bleaching become stronger and less vulnerable to later heat waves.
Kaleo explains that bleaching occurs when corals expel the algae that live inside their tissue.
RW2.explain: The main idea holds both halves: moderate past heat seemed protective, severe past bleaching didn’t (it may have hurt). B drops Kaleo’s caution. C reverses it. D is a background detail from the first two sentences.

RW2.passage:
The following text is from a novel. Rahel, a translator, is working on a difficult passage.

The sentence was eleven words long in the original, and Rahel had been staring at it for an hour. Its meaning was not the problem; she could have explained it to a child. The problem was its rhythm, which rose through the first nine words and then fell, all at once, on the last two. Every English version she tried either kept the meaning and flattened the fall, or kept the fall and lost the sense of the middle clause.
RW2.stem: According to the text, what is the main difficulty Rahel faces in translating the sentence?
choices: She cannot find English words that match the final two words of the original.
She does not fully understand what the sentence means.
She cannot preserve both the sentence’s meaning and its rhythm in English.
The sentence is too long to translate as a single English sentence.
RW2.explain: The last sentence lays out the bind: each version keeps meaning or rhythm, never both. B is contradicted (“Its meaning was not the problem”). A narrows the problem to two words, though the issue is the fall across the whole sentence. D isn’t suggested by an eleven-word sentence.

RW2.passage: Sociologist Daniel Ferreira hypothesizes that the decline in local newspaper subscriptions in the towns he studied was caused mainly by the growth of free online news rather than by changes in the newspapers themselves.
RW2.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Ferreira’s hypothesis?
choices: Subscriptions fell fastest in the towns where high-speed internet became available earliest.
Among towns with similar internet access, subscriptions fell sharply where newspapers cut their reporting staffs by more than half and held roughly steady where newspapers kept their staffs.
Most former subscribers said in surveys that they now read news online.
Subscriptions to national newspapers also declined during the period Ferreira studied.
RW2.explain: B holds internet access constant and still finds the decline tracking cuts at the papers themselves, which points to the newspapers’ own changes and against online news as the main cause. A and C fit the hypothesis (they support it). D is about national papers, a different question.

RW2.passage: In the poem “Inventory,” the speaker suggests that ordinary objects can call up memories more vividly than photographs do.
RW2.stem: Which quotation from the poem most effectively illustrates the claim?
choices: “The photographs are in a box I rarely open; / they show us squinting into other summers.”
“My father’s reading glasses on the sill / bring back his voice more surely than any picture of his face.”
“I kept the chipped blue bowl, the broken clock, / the coat that still hangs crooked on its hook.”
“Each picture fixes one afternoon in place, / the light exactly as it fell that day.”
RW2.explain: The claim is a comparison: objects beat photographs at calling up memory. B makes it: the glasses bring back his voice “more surely than any picture.” C lists objects but makes no comparison and recalls nothing. D praises photographs, the opposite emphasis. A mentions photographs but not objects.

RW2.passage: Marine biologists grew young bull kelp and giant kelp in tanks held at three temperatures. They suggest that giant kelp may be better suited than bull kelp to warming coastal waters.
RW2.stem: Which choice best describes data from the table that support the biologists’ suggestion?
choices: At 10°C, bull kelp grew slightly faster than giant kelp, 6.1 cm per day compared with 5.9.
Bull kelp grew fastest at 15°C, at 6.4 cm per day.
At 15°C, giant kelp grew faster than bull kelp, 6.6 cm per day compared with 6.4.
The two species grew at similar rates at 10°C, but at 20°C giant kelp grew 6.2 cm per day while bull kelp’s growth fell to 3.2.

Average growth of young kelp (cm per day)
Water temperatureBull kelpGiant kelp
10°C6.15.9

RW2.explain: “Warming” means the evidence must show what happens as temperature rises. D does: similar at 10°C, a wide gap at 20°C as bull kelp slows. C shows a 0.2 cm advantage at a middle temperature, too small and too partial to carry the claim. A favors bull kelp. B is about one species only.

RW2.passage: Biologists recorded the day of the year when ice left a northern lake each spring (ice-out) and the average spring arrival day of two migratory bird species. They claim that tree swallows have shifted their arrival to track the earlier ice-out, but yellow warblers have not.
RW2.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support the claim?
choices: Yellow warblers arrived later than tree swallows in every year shown.
From 1990 to 2020, ice-out moved about 17 days earlier and tree swallow arrival moved about 16 days earlier, while yellow warbler arrival stayed near day 128.
Tree swallows arrived before ice-out in every year shown.
Ice-out moved from about day 118 in 1990 to about day 101 in 2020.
RW2.explain: The claim compares two species against the ice-out trend. B shows all three lines: ice-out and swallows shifting together by similar amounts, warblers flat. A and C are accurate comparisons that don’t address change over time. D describes ice-out alone.

RW2.passage: Researchers analyzing residues inside 5,000-year-old ceramic jars from a site in northern China found traces of barley, millet, and an edible tuber, along with chemical signs of fermentation. Elsewhere in the region, barley does not appear as a significant food crop until several thousand years later. The researchers suggest that
RW2.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: barley was the main food crop at the site 5,000 years ago.
barley may first have been brought to the region for brewing rather than as a staple food.
people at the site did not yet know how to ferment grains.
the jars must have been made somewhere other than northern China.
RW2.explain: Barley shows up in fermentation residues long before it becomes a regular food crop, so its earliest use there may have been for brewing. A contradicts the later arrival as a food crop. C contradicts the fermentation evidence. D has no support.

RW2.passage: In a study of red foxes in a large city, researchers found that foxes living in neighborhoods with many backyard gardens had smaller home ranges than foxes in neighborhoods with few gardens. One explanation is that gardens supply food, so foxes there need not travel far. However, foxes in neighborhoods where residents deliberately fed them had home ranges no smaller than those of foxes in neighborhoods with few gardens, even though the fed foxes got a larger share of their diet from people than garden-neighborhood foxes did. These findings suggest that
RW2.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: foxes that are fed by residents travel farther than other urban foxes.
backyard gardens provide more food for foxes than residents deliberately provide.
some feature of gardens other than the food they provide may account for the smaller home ranges.
urban foxes avoid neighborhoods where residents feed them.
RW2.explain: If food alone shrank home ranges, the heavily fed foxes should have small ranges too, and they didn’t. So something else about gardens (shelter, cover) is the likelier cause. B is ruled out by the last clause: fed foxes got more food from people. A turns “no smaller” into “larger.” D has no support.

RW2.passage: Ada Lovelace, the daughter of the poet Lord Byron, who left the family when she was an infant,  what many historians regard as the first published computer program in 1843.
RW2.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: writing
having written
to write
wrote
RW2.explain: The subject is Ada Lovelace; after the appositive and the “who” clause (which describes Byron), the sentence still needs its main verb. Only wrote is finite.

RW2.passage: Sea otters often wrap themselves in strands of kelp while they  drifting away from their feeding grounds as they rest on the surface.
RW2.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: sleep, keeping themselves from
sleep, they keep themselves from
sleep, kept themselves from
sleep, to have kept themselves from
RW2.explain: “Sea otters … wrap themselves” is the main clause, so the phrase after the comma is a modifier telling what the wrapping does, and it takes the -ing form. B is a comma splice. C is a finite verb with no subject. D’s perfect infinitive puts the action in the wrong time.

RW2.passage: The expedition reached the summit on its third  the weather allowed the climbers only twenty minutes at the top.
RW2.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: attempt, however,
attempt however,
attempt; however,
attempt, however
RW2.explain: “However” begins the second of two complete clauses, so the clauses need a semicolon before it, with a comma after it. A and D splice the clauses with commas; B has no boundary punctuation.

RW2.passage: The number of languages spoken in Papua New Guinea, a country slightly larger than California,  more than 800.
RW2.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: are
have been
were
is
RW2.explain: “The number of” is singular (one number), so the verb is singular: is. “Languages” is the object of the preposition. (Compare “a number of languages are.”)

RW2.passage: The tiny backward-facing spines that cover the surface of a cat’s  help it groom by catching loose fur.
RW2.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: tongue,
tongue;
tongue
tongue—
RW2.explain: The subject is the long phrase “The tiny … spines that cover the surface of a cat’s tongue,” and its verb is “help.” No punctuation goes between a subject and its verb, however long the subject. A, B, and D all split them.

RW2.passage: When the museum reopened in 2022 after a four-year renovation, visitors discovered that the curators  the galleries by theme rather than by historical period.
RW2.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: had rearranged
rearrange
will rearrange
are rearranging
RW2.explain: The rearranging was finished before the visitors discovered it in 2022, so it takes the past perfect: had rearranged. B and D are present tense, and C future, for a past event.

RW2.passage: The coast  can grow to more than 110 meters in height.
RW2.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: redwood—the tallest tree species on Earth—
redwood, the tallest tree species on Earth—
redwood—the tallest tree species on Earth,
redwood the tallest tree species on Earth,
RW2.explain: The appositive (“the tallest tree species on Earth”) interrupts the subject and its verb, so it needs matching punctuation on both sides: two dashes. B and C mix a comma with a dash. D omits the opening punctuation.

RW2.passage: Early telescopes made with lenses suffered from chromatic aberration: because a lens bends different colors of light by different amounts, the images were fringed with color. Isaac Newton concluded that the problem could not be fully solved with lenses.  he built a telescope that gathered light with a curved mirror, which reflects all colors at the same angle.
RW2.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices: Similarly,
Nevertheless,
Instead,
For example,
RW2.explain: Having given up on lenses, Newton used a mirror in their place: instead. “Nevertheless” would mean he built the mirror telescope despite concluding lenses couldn’t work, which gets the logic backward; the conclusion is his reason for the mirror.

RW2.passage: The Voynich manuscript, a fifteenth-century book written in an unknown script, has resisted every attempt at decipherment, and some researchers have concluded that it is an elaborate hoax.  statistical analyses show that its “words” follow patterns of frequency and repetition much like those of natural languages, which a hoaxer of that period would have found very difficult to fake.
RW2.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices: Accordingly,
Likewise,
For instance,
Still,
RW2.explain: The statistics cut against the hoax conclusion, so the transition must signal contrast: still (meaning “even so”). “Accordingly” and “likewise” treat the evidence as agreeing with the hoax theory. “For instance” makes it an example of it.

RW2.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • Builders at Chaco Canyon in present-day New Mexico aligned some of its great houses with the position of the sun at the solstices.
  • Builders at Newgrange in Ireland designed a passage tomb so that sunlight enters its inner chamber at sunrise on the winter solstice.
  • Chaco Canyon’s great houses were built between about 850 and 1150 CE.
  • Newgrange was built around 3200 BCE.
RW2.stem: The student wants to emphasize a similarity between the two sites. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: While Chaco Canyon’s great houses were built between about 850 and 1150 CE, Newgrange was built around 3200 BCE.
Like Newgrange, which was built around 3200 BCE, Chaco Canyon’s great houses were built more than four thousand years later.
At both Chaco Canyon and Newgrange, builders designed structures to align with the sun at the solstices.
Newgrange is a passage tomb in Ireland, whereas Chaco Canyon is known for its great houses.
RW2.explain: C states the shared feature: solar alignment at the solstices. B opens with “Like,” a similarity word, but its actual content is a difference in dates. A and D are differences outright.

RW2.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • Coffee, tea, and cacao plants all produce caffeine.
  • Coffee plants evolved the ability to make caffeine independently of tea and cacao plants.
  • Caffeine in a plant’s leaves deters many insects that would otherwise eat them.
  • Caffeine that leaches into the soil from fallen leaves can slow the growth of nearby seedlings, reducing competition.
RW2.stem: The student wants to summarize two ways caffeine may benefit the plants that produce it. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: Caffeine may help the plants that produce it by deterring leaf-eating insects and by slowing the growth of competing seedlings nearby.
Coffee plants evolved the ability to make caffeine independently of tea and cacao, and caffeine deters many leaf-eating insects.
Caffeine may help nearby seedlings grow and may deter insects from eating a plant’s leaves.
Coffee, tea, and cacao plants all produce caffeine, which leaches into the soil from their fallen leaves.
RW2.explain: The goal asks for two benefits. A gives both. B gives one benefit plus a fact about evolution. C reverses the second benefit (caffeine slows nearby seedlings). D gives no benefit at all.

RW2.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • In 2015, paleontologists announced the discovery of fossils of a new human relative, Homo naledi, in a South African cave.
  • Homo naledi had a brain less than half the size of a modern human’s.
  • Before the fossils were dated, many researchers assumed that a species with such a small brain must have lived more than a million years ago.
  • The fossils were later dated to between 236,000 and 335,000 years ago.
RW2.stem: The student wants to emphasize why the dating of the fossils surprised researchers. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: Surprisingly, the fossils of Homo naledi were found in a cave in South Africa.
Homo naledi fossils, discovered in South Africa in 2015, were dated to between 236,000 and 335,000 years ago.
Because Homo naledi had such a small brain, researchers dated its fossils to more than a million years ago.

Although Homo naledi had a brain less than half the size of a modern human’s, its fossils proved to be only 236,000 to 335,000 years old, far younger than many researchers had expected for so small-brained a species.
RW2.explain: The surprise is the mismatch between a small brain (which suggested great age) and a young date. D states both and says it was unexpected. A uses “surprisingly” about the location, which wasn’t the surprise. B gives the date without the expectation it overturned. C misreports the notes: the million-year figure was an assumption, not the dating result.

M1.stem: A car’s value decreases by 15% each year. The car was bought for $28,000. Which expression gives the car’s value, in dollars, m months after it was bought?

28,000(0.85)m/12

M1.stem: A phone plan costs $30 per month plus $0.10 for each text message after the first 200 texts in a month. Kai wants his bill to be at most $45 this month. What is the greatest number of text messages Kai can send this month?
choices: 150
450
650

M1.explain: 30+0.10(t−200)≤45 gives t−200≤150, so t≤350. Choice A is the number of extra texts; the first 200 are free.

M1.stem: A circle in the xy-plane has its center at (−2,5) and passes through the point (4,−3). Which of the following is an equation of the circle?

(x+2)2+(y−5)2=10

M1.stem: A plant grew at a constant rate after it was potted. It was 12 centimeters tall 4 days after it was potted and 27 centimeters tall 10 days after it was potted. How tall, in centimeters, was the plant when it was potted?

M1.explain: Let the width be w: 2(w+2w+4)=50, so 3w+4=25 and w=7. The length is 18, and the area is 7×18=126.

M1.explain: One solution means the discriminant is zero: (−12)2−4(2)(c)=144−8c=0, so c=18.

M1.stem: The function f is defined by f(x)=x2+bx+20, where b is a constant, and the function g is defined by g(x)=f(x−3). If the vertex of the graph of y=g(x) in the xy-plane has an x-coordinate of 5, what is the value of b?

M2.stem: A tank that holds 200 gallons contains 40 gallons of water. Water flows in at 3.5 gallons per minute and drains out at 1.2 gallons per minute at the same time. To the nearest minute, how many minutes will it take for the tank to become full?

M2.stem: Two cones are similar. The height of the larger cone is 1.5 times the height of the smaller cone. The volume of the smaller cone is 64π cubic centimeters. What is the volume, in cubic centimeters, of the larger cone?

M2.stem: The function P(t)=5,000(1.02)4t models the value, in dollars, of an investment t years after it was made. Which statement best describes how the value changes?

It increases by 8% each year.

M2.stem: A researcher randomly assigned 300 adult volunteers to two groups. One group drank a cup of green tea every evening for a month, and the other drank a cup of water. The green tea group reported better sleep, on average, and the difference was unlikely to be due to chance. Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: Drinking green tea every evening causes better sleep for all adults.
Among adults similar to the volunteers, drinking green tea every evening is likely to cause better reported sleep.
The volunteers who chose to drink green tea were probably better sleepers to begin with.
No conclusion about cause can be drawn, because the study used a sample rather than the whole population.
M2.explain: Random assignment supports a causal conclusion; using volunteers limits it to people like them. A overgeneralizes to all adults. C ignores that the groups were assigned randomly, not chosen. D is wrong: random assignment is exactly what lets a sample support cause.

M2.stem: In the xy-plane, the graphs of y=2x2−5 and y=kx−7, where k is a constant, intersect at exactly one point, and that point has a positive x-coordinate. What is the value of k?
M2.explain: Set equal: 2x2−kx+2=0. One intersection needs a zero discriminant: k2−16=0, so k=±4. The single solution is x=4k​, which is positive only when k=4.

M2.stem: In the xy-plane, an angle of θ radians is drawn in standard position, where π<θ<23π​, and sinθ=−135​. What is the value of tanθ?
choices: −125​
125​
−512​
512​
M2.explain: In the third quadrant both sine and cosine are negative, so cosθ=−1312​ and tanθ=−12/13−5/13​=125​. Choice A gets the sign wrong; C and D invert the ratio.

M2.stem: A school needs at least 40 calculators. Basic calculators cost $18 each and graphing calculators cost $95 each. The school can spend at most $2,000 and wants at least 10 graphing calculators. What is the greatest number of graphing calculators the school can buy?
choices: 16
17
20
21
M2.explain: To maximize graphing calculators, buy the fewest basic ones: 40−g. Then 18(40−g)+95g≤2,000, so 77g≤1,280 and g≤16.6. The answer is 16. Choice D spends the whole budget on graphing calculators and ignores the 40-calculator requirement; B rounds up past the limit.

M2.stem: A store took 20% off the original price of a jacket. Then an 8% sales tax was added to the sale price, for a total of $86.40. What was the original price of the jacket, in dollars?
M2.explain: p(0.80)(1.08)=0.864p=86.40, so p=100. Adding and subtracting the percents (p×0.88) gives a wrong answer.

M2.stem: What is the solution set of the equation x+7​=x−5?
choices: {2}
{9}
{2,9}
{−2,−9}
M2.explain: Square: x+7=x2−10x+25, so x2−11x+18=0 and x=2 or x=9. Check: at x=9, 16​=4=9−5. At x=2, 9​=3 but 2−5=−3, so 2 is extraneous. Choice C keeps it.

M2.stem: A square is inscribed in a circle with radius 6, as shown. What is the area of the shaded region, which is inside the circle but outside the square?
choices: 36π−144
36π−36
144−36π
36π−72
M2.explain: The square’s diagonal is the diameter, 12, so its area is 2122​=72. The circle’s area is 36π. Shaded: 36π−72. Choice A uses 122 as the square’s area, as if its side were 12.

M2.stem: The function f is defined by f(x)=ax2+bx+c. If f(−1)=0, f(3)=0, and f(1)=−8, what is the value of f(4)?
M2.explain: The zeros give f(x)=a(x+1)(x−3). Then f(1)=a(2)(−2)=−4a=−8, so a=2, and f(4)=2(5)(1)=10.

M2.stem: Class A has 18 students, and their mean score on a test was 82. Class B’s mean score on the same test was 87. The mean score of all the students in both classes combined was 84. How many students are in class B?
choices: 8
10
12
15
M2.explain: 82(18)+87n=84(18+n) gives 1,476+87n=1,512+84n, so 3n=36 and n=12.

M2.stem: The function f is defined by f(x)=a(x+2)(x−6), where a is a constant, and f(0)=−6. What is the minimum value of f?
choices: −8
−6
−12
−16
M2.explain: f(0)=a(2)(−6)=−12a=−6, so a=21​. The vertex is midway between the zeros, at x=2: f(2)=21​(4)(−4)=−8. Choice B is the y-intercept, not the minimum.

RW1.passage: The new footbridge’s design is deliberately : its cables and deck are painted the same gray-green as the surrounding forest, so that from the river below it nearly disappears.
RW1.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: ornate
inconspicuous
temporary
symmetrical
RW1.explain: A bridge painted to blend into the forest so it “nearly disappears” is meant not to be noticed: inconspicuous. Ornate is the opposite. Nothing concerns how long it will stand (temporary) or its shape (symmetrical).

RW1.passage: Microbiologist Teresa Okoye’s findings  the long-standing view that the bacteria are harmless: she showed that in large numbers they release a toxin that damages the gills of farmed salmon.
RW1.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: reinforce
clarify
anticipate
challenge
RW1.explain: A toxin that damages gills contradicts “harmless,” so the findings challenge the view. Reinforce reverses the relationship. Clarify is too mild for evidence that overturns a view.

RW1.passage:
The following text is from a novel. Teodoro is learning to play the cello from his aunt.

His aunt listened to the scale without comment. Then she took the bow from him and played it herself, slowly, letting each note settle before she moved to the next, and when she handed the bow back he understood that she had not been correcting his fingers at all.
RW1.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “settle” most nearly mean?
choices: pay off
move into
come to rest
make a decision
RW1.explain: She lets each note settle before the next, letting the sound finish and come to rest. “Pay off” (settle a debt), “move into” (settle a region), and “make a decision” (settle a question) are other senses of the word that don’t apply to a musical note.

RW1.passage: The senator’s response to the report was : she neither endorsed nor criticized its findings, saying only that her office would need more time to review them.
RW1.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: noncommittal
dismissive
enthusiastic
belated
RW1.explain: Neither endorsing nor criticizing, and deferring judgment, is noncommittal. Dismissive would require rejecting or brushing off the findings, which she doesn’t do. Enthusiastic contradicts “neither endorsed.”

RW1.passage: Glass frogs of Central America are nearly transparent, and while they sleep they become two to three times more transparent than when they are active. Red blood cells strongly absorb light, so biologists wondered where the frogs’ blood goes. Using an imaging technique that tracks blood cells without harming the animal, researchers found that a sleeping frog packs nearly 90 percent of its red blood cells into its liver. How the frogs avoid dangerous clotting with so many cells crowded together remains unknown.
RW1.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
choices: It describes a puzzling feature of an animal, explains what researchers discovered about it, and notes a question that remains open.
It presents two competing explanations for a feature of an animal, then explains which one the evidence favors.
It describes an experiment that failed to answer a question and proposes a new method for answering it.
It introduces an animal, compares it with a related species, and summarizes the animal’s evolutionary history.
RW1.explain: Puzzle (where does the blood go while the frogs sleep?), discovery (90 percent in the liver), open question (how they avoid clotting). B invents two competing explanations; C invents a failed experiment; D invents a comparison species.

RW1.passage: Many cities plant street trees to shade and cool their neighborhoods. Planners in Melbourne, Australia, went a step further: <u>they gave each of the city’s tens of thousands of trees an identification number and an email address so that residents could report damaged branches or disease.</u> To the planners’ surprise, residents also used the addresses to write letters to their favorite trees, thanking them for their shade or simply saying hello.
RW1.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined portion in the text as a whole?
choices: It explains how street trees cool city neighborhoods.
It describes a practical measure whose unexpected use is reported in the next sentence.
It provides evidence that Melbourne has more street trees than most other cities.
It criticizes the planners for spending money on an unnecessary program.
RW1.explain: The underlined portion describes the email system and its intended purpose (reporting problems); the next sentence reports the surprise use (letters to trees). It doesn’t explain cooling (A), compare cities (C), or criticize anyone (D).

RW1.passage:
Text 1
Many music teachers argue that children should learn to read musical notation before they learn to play by ear. Notation, they point out, opens up centuries of written repertoire, and students who first learn by ear may come to rely on it and struggle to read music later.

Text 2
Music education researcher Ola Brekke followed two groups of young violin students for two years. One group learned songs by ear first and began reading notation after six months; the other began with notation. By the end of the study, the two groups read music equally accurately, and the ear-first group improvised with noticeably more confidence.
RW1.stem: Based on the texts, how would Brekke (Text 2) most likely respond to the concern raised by the music teachers in Text 1?
choices: By arguing that reading notation is less important than the teachers suggest
By agreeing that ear-first students struggle to read music but noting that they improvise better
By pointing out that, in her study, learning by ear first did not leave students worse at reading music
By suggesting that the teachers have underestimated how much written repertoire exists
RW1.explain: The teachers worry that ear-first students will struggle to read. Brekke found equal reading accuracy after two years, so that worry didn’t come true in her study. B contradicts that finding. A goes beyond her: she never downplays notation. D isn’t addressed.

RW1.passage: Bowhead whales can live for more than 200 years. Biologists long assumed that a large, long-lived animal should be especially prone to cancer, since more cells dividing over more years means more chances for harmful mutations. Yet bowheads rarely develop cancer. Biologist Yusuf Demir found that bowhead cells repair broken DNA unusually accurately, which suggests that the whales’ defense lies less in destroying damaged cells than in fixing the damage before it leads to disease.
RW1.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Demir’s research suggests that bowhead whales avoid cancer largely by accurately repairing DNA damage.
Biologists have shown that large animals are no more likely than small animals to develop cancer.
Bowhead whales live longer than any other mammal because they rarely develop cancer.
Bowhead whale cells destroy damaged cells more efficiently than the cells of other animals do.
RW1.explain: The text sets up a puzzle (long-lived but cancer-resistant) and gives Demir’s answer (accurate DNA repair). D reverses his conclusion: the defense lies less in destroying damaged cells. C invents a “longest-lived” claim and a causal link. B generalizes far past one species.

RW1.passage: The town of Kiruna, in northern Sweden, sits above one of the world’s largest underground iron ore mines. Because mining beneath the town has caused the ground to crack and shift, the town center is being relocated about three kilometers to the east. A few buildings, including a wooden church built in 1912, have been lifted whole and carried to the new site on enormous trailers; most of the others are being torn down and rebuilt.
RW1.stem: According to the text, why is Kiruna’s town center being relocated?
choices: Mining beneath the town has caused the ground to crack and shift.
Many of the town’s buildings were too old to be repaired.
The iron ore mine beneath the town has closed.
A new mine is being dug to the east of the town.
RW1.explain: The second sentence gives the reason: the ground is cracking because of the mining. B misreads why buildings are rebuilt rather than moved. C contradicts the ongoing mining. D invents a new mine; the town moves east, but nothing says a mine is there.

RW1.passage: Historian Grace Liu argues that the popularity of public libraries in small American towns in the late nineteenth century owed less to a desire for self-education than to a demand for novels.
RW1.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Liu’s argument?
choices: The number of public libraries in small towns more than doubled between 1875 and 1900.
Many small-town libraries hosted public lectures on science and history.
Circulation records from several small-town libraries show that novels made up about three-quarters of all books borrowed, while instructional works made up less than a tenth.
Librarians in several towns wrote that patrons should read more serious books.
RW1.explain: Liu compares two motives, so support should compare what patrons actually borrowed. C does: novels dwarfed instructional books. A shows popularity without explaining it. B points toward self-education, which cuts against her. D hints at fiction reading but is only librarians’ opinion, much weaker than borrowing records.

RW1.passage: In a play, the character Mara reveals that she resents her brother’s success even as she praises him.
RW1.stem: Which quotation from the play most effectively illustrates the claim?
choices: “He worked harder than any of us. I watched him study at the kitchen table every night for four years.”
“Of course I’m proud of him. Everyone is proud of him. I hear about it at the grocery store, at the dentist, from strangers who have never met either of us.”
“I moved back to this town because the rent was cheap and I missed the river.”
“The last time he visited, he brought flowers for Mother and stayed for an hour.”
RW1.explain: B opens with praise (“proud of him”) and then lets weariness at hearing about him everywhere show through: praise and resentment together. A is praise only. C and D say nothing about his success.

RW1.passage: Students studied lists of unfamiliar words using one of three methods and were tested after one day and after one week. The researchers concluded that the advantage of self-testing over rereading grows as time passes.
RW1.stem: Which choice best describes data from the table that support the researchers’ conclusion?
choices: Self-testing produced the highest recall of the three methods both after one day and after one week.
Recall declined from one day to one week for all three methods.
Highlighting produced the lowest recall of the three methods at both times.
Self-testing led rereading by 4 percentage points after one day (66 vs 62) but by 21 points after one week (55 vs 34).
RW1.figure:
Percentage of vocabulary words recalled
Study methodAfter 1 dayAfter 1 week
Rereading6234
Highlighting5830
Self-testing6655
RW1.explain: “Advantage grows” means the gap between self-testing and rereading widens. D computes both gaps: 4 points, then 21. A shows self-testing winning but not the gap growing. B and C don’t compare self-testing with rereading.

RW1.passage: In sea turtles, the temperature of the sand around a nest determines the sex of the hatchlings. At one nesting beach, average nest temperatures have risen from about 29°C to about 30°C over recent decades, and researchers predict a sharp rise in the share of female hatchlings:
RW1.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?
choices: at 27°C, only about 5% of hatchlings were female.
at 29°C, about half of hatchlings were female, but at 30°C about 80% were.
at 30°C, about 20% of hatchlings were female.
at 31°C, nearly all hatchlings were female.
RW1.explain: The prediction concerns the beach’s actual change, from 29°C to 30°C. B gives the female share at both: 50% rising to 80%. A and D describe temperatures outside that range. C misreads the graph (20% is the value at 28°C).

RW1.passage: Most wild bananas are full of hard seeds. The bananas sold in grocery stores, by contrast, are seedless, so they cannot be grown from seed; new plants are grown instead from shoots cut from existing plants. As a result, nearly all the plants of a given commercial variety are genetically identical. A disease that can infect one plant of such a variety is therefore likely to
RW1.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: be able to infect most other plants of the same variety.
be easily cured by planting new shoots.
spread only through the seeds of wild bananas.
leave wild bananas unharmed.
RW1.explain: Genetically identical plants share the same vulnerabilities, so a disease that infects one can probably infect the rest. C contradicts the seedless setup. B ignores that new shoots are clones, just as vulnerable. D draws a conclusion about wild bananas the text doesn’t support.

RW1.passage: In many unrelated languages, the everyday word for “mother” begins with an m sound, as in mama, and the word for “father” often begins with p, b, t, or d. One explanation is that these are among the first consonants infants produce, and parents tend to take an infant’s early babbling as referring to them. If this explanation is correct, words for “mother” and “father” would be expected to
RW1.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: be identical in every language.
resemble infants’ early sounds more often than words for other relatives do.
be among the last words that children learn to say.
have been borrowed by most languages from a single ancient language.
RW1.explain: If parents shape these words around babbling, the words should look like early infant sounds more than ordinary kinship words do. A overstates (“identical in every language”). C contradicts the idea that these come from the earliest sounds. D offers a different explanation, borrowing, rather than following from this one.

RW1.passage: The James Webb Space Telescope, which orbits the Sun about 1.5 million kilometers from Earth and observes mainly in infrared light,  images of galaxies that formed less than 400 million years after the big bang.
RW1.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: capturing
having captured
to capture
has captured
RW1.explain: Subject: The James Webb Space Telescope. The “which” clause has its own verbs (orbits, observes), but the main clause still needs one. Only has captured is finite.

RW1.passage: The novel  was rejected by eleven publishers before a small press in Minneapolis accepted it.
RW1.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: that she considers her best,
—that she considers her best—
that she considers her best
, that she considers her best,
RW1.explain: “That she considers her best” identifies which novel (she has others), so it’s essential, and essential clauses take no commas or dashes. A puts a comma between the subject and its verb. B and D set the clause off as if it were nonessential, which “that” clauses never are.

RW1.passage: Each of the forty volunteers who counted birds along the river  a different stretch of the shoreline.
RW1.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: were assigned
was assigned
are assigned
have been assigned
RW1.explain: The subject is each, which is singular; “of the forty volunteers who counted birds along the river” is a modifier. A, C, and D are plural, matching “volunteers.”

RW1.passage: Every spring, the town’s two  compete to see whose float will win the parade’s top prize.
RW1.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: high school’s
high schools’
high schools
high schools’s
RW1.explain: The schools don’t possess anything here; they’re the subject of “compete,” so the plain plural high schools is right. A and B are possessives. D isn’t a standard form.

RW1.passage: In 1971 the United States Congress passed a law  wild horses and burros living on public lands.
RW1.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: protects
and protects
it protected
protecting
RW1.explain: The sentence already has its subject and verb (Congress passed). The blank begins a phrase describing the law, which needs the nonfinite protecting. A, B, and C add finite verbs that can’t attach: A has no subject; C creates a second clause with no connector; B shifts to present tense for a 1971 event.

RW1.passage: The first expedition failed to reach the cave’s lowest  the second, equipped with better ropes and lights, mapped it completely.
RW1.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: chamber; but,
chamber but,
chamber,
chamber, but
RW1.explain: Two complete clauses joined by “but” need a comma before the conjunction. A puts a semicolon before “but” and a comma after it, which is incorrect. C is a comma splice. B misplaces the comma after “but.”

RW1.passage: By the time a vaccine became widely available in 1955, polio  thousands of American children every year for decades.
RW1.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices: had paralyzed
paralyzes
will paralyze
is paralyzing
RW1.explain: “By the time” plus a past event (1955) calls for an action completed before that point: the past perfect had paralyzed. B and D are present tense and C is future, which don’t fit a historical period.

RW1.passage: The first transatlantic telegraph cable, completed in 1858, carried messages for only about three weeks before it failed.  a more durable cable laid in 1866 operated for years and cut the time for news to cross between Europe and North America from about ten days to a matter of minutes.
RW1.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices: Similarly,
Therefore,
For example,
By contrast,
RW1.explain: A cable that failed in weeks is set against one that worked for years: by contrast. “Similarly” implies the cables performed alike. “Therefore” makes the 1866 success a consequence of the 1858 failure, which the text doesn’t claim.

RW1.passage: Mosquitoes locate people partly by detecting the carbon dioxide in exhaled breath, which they can sense from many meters away. Once a mosquito is within about a meter of a person,  carbon dioxide matters less: the insect relies instead on body heat and skin odors to choose where to land.
RW1.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices: therefore,
for example,
however,
moreover,
RW1.explain: At a distance carbon dioxide guides the mosquito; up close it “matters less.” That shift is a contrast: however. “Moreover” would add a further point in the same direction, and “therefore” would make the close-range change a result of the long-range sensing.

RW1.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • Deception Pass Bridge connects Whidbey Island and Fidalgo Island in Washington State.
  • It was completed in 1935.
  • The bridge spans a narrow channel where tidal currents can exceed 8 knots.
  • Deception Pass State Park, which surrounds the bridge, is one of Washington’s most visited state parks.
RW1.stem: The student wants to introduce Deception Pass Bridge to an audience unfamiliar with it. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: Deception Pass State Park is one of Washington’s most visited state parks.
Tidal currents in the narrow channel beneath the bridge can exceed 8 knots.
Deception Pass Bridge, completed in 1935, connects Whidbey Island and Fidalgo Island in Washington State, spanning a narrow channel with powerful tidal currents.
The bridge was completed in 1935, and the state park around it is very popular.
RW1.explain: An introduction tells an unfamiliar reader what the thing is and where. C names the bridge, its location, what it connects, and its setting. A and B describe the park and the currents without introducing the bridge. D says “the bridge” as if the reader already knew which one.

RW1.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • Mercury and Venus are the two planets closest to the Sun.
  • Neither Mercury nor Venus has a moon.
  • Mercury has almost no atmosphere.
  • Venus has a thick atmosphere made mostly of carbon dioxide.
RW1.stem: The student wants to emphasize a difference between the two planets’ atmospheres. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: Unlike Venus, Mercury has no moon.
Mercury has almost no atmosphere, whereas Venus has a thick atmosphere made mostly of carbon dioxide.
Mercury and Venus, the two planets closest to the Sun, both lack moons.
Venus has a thick atmosphere made mostly of carbon dioxide.
RW1.explain: B contrasts the atmospheres directly. A uses “unlike” for a feature the planets share (neither has a moon), so its content contradicts the notes. C is a similarity. D describes only Venus.

RW1.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
  • The Atacama Desert in northern Chile is one of the driest places on Earth.
  • Several major astronomical observatories are located there.
  • Water vapor in the air absorbs some of the infrared light that many telescopes are designed to detect.
  • The Atacama’s high altitude and frequent clear skies also benefit astronomers.
RW1.stem: The student wants to explain why the Atacama’s dryness benefits astronomers. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices: Because the Atacama’s dry air holds little water vapor, which absorbs infrared light, telescopes there can detect more of that light.
The Atacama’s high altitude and frequent clear skies benefit astronomers.
Several major astronomical observatories are located in the Atacama Desert, one of the driest places on Earth.
Because water vapor helps telescopes detect infrared light, observatories have been built in the Atacama Desert.
RW1.explain: A links dryness to less water vapor to more infrared light reaching telescopes, which is the explanation the goal asks for. B gives other benefits, not dryness. C states facts without explaining. D reverses the role of water vapor.

RW2.passage: Scholars once regarded the poet’s letters as merely  to her poems, useful mainly for dating when each poem was written; more recent critics, however, read the letters as literary works in their own right.
RW2.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: ancillary
superior
antithetical
identical
RW2.explain: “Merely,” plus “useful mainly for dating” the poems, casts the letters as secondary aids: ancillary. “Superior” reverses the ranking. “Antithetical” (opposed) and “identical” don’t describe a supporting role.

RW2.passage: The documentary’s portrait of the celebrated chef is far from : it lingers on her temper, her failed restaurants, and her quarrels with former partners as much as on her triumphs.
RW2.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: critical
hagiographic
balanced
fragmentary
RW2.explain: The film gives her flaws as much time as her triumphs, so it is not an idealizing tribute: far from hagiographic. “Far from critical” and “far from balanced” flip the meaning, since dwelling on flaws is critical, and equal time for flaws and triumphs is balanced.

RW2.passage:
The following text is from a novel. Lucia is reading a letter from her sister, with whom she has not spoken in eleven years.

The letter was cordial, even warm, and Lucia read it three times looking for the barb. She found none. That, she decided at last, was the barb: after eleven years of silence, her sister had written as though nothing needed to be
RW2.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: acknowledged.
concealed.
celebrated.
repeated.
RW2.explain: The sting is the letter’s silence about the eleven-year rift: the sister writes as if nothing needed to be acknowledged. “Concealed” reverses it: the problem is that the rift goes unmentioned, not that something is hidden on purpose. “Celebrated” and “repeated” don’t capture the omission.

RW2.passage: Rather than  the review committee’s objections, the engineer’s revised proposal confronts each one, devoting a full section to every concern the committee raised.
RW2.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices: sidestep
document
echo
anticipate
RW2.explain: “Rather than” sets up the opposite of confronting: avoiding, or sidestepping. “Document” isn’t opposite to confronting (a section per concern documents them). “Anticipate” doesn’t fit objections already raised.

RW2.passage: In the 1950s, many economists predicted that automation would soon leave large numbers of workers permanently unemployed. <u>Employment in manufacturing did eventually fall, but total employment kept rising as new kinds of jobs appeared.</u> Economist Liesel Varga argues that this history should make today’s forecasters cautious, though not complacent: past patterns, she notes, do not guarantee that new jobs will appear as quickly in the future.
RW2.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
choices: It presents an outcome that only partly matched an earlier prediction.
It provides evidence that the economists’ prediction was entirely correct.
It states the conclusion that Varga draws about today’s forecasts.
It explains why automation has had no effect on employment.
RW2.explain: Manufacturing jobs fell (as predicted) but total employment rose (not as predicted): a partial match. B ignores the second half. C is the job of the next sentence. D contradicts “employment in manufacturing did eventually fall.”

RW2.passage:
The following text is from a poem.

My uncle read the water like a page:
the darker seams where currents crossed, the gulls
that sat too long on pilings. He’d turn home
an hour before the forecast caught the wind,
and never once explained how he could tell.
RW2.stem: Which choice best describes the overall purpose of the text?
choices: To explain how currents and the behavior of gulls can be used to predict storms
To criticize the uncle for ignoring official weather forecasts
To convey that the uncle’s skill rested on knowledge he never put into words
To express the speaker’s fear of being caught at sea in bad weather
RW2.explain: The poem shows the uncle reading signs better than the forecast and ends on the fact that he “never once explained how he could tell.” A is the trap: the poem lists signs but doesn’t explain how they predict anything. B misreads him: he outperforms the forecast rather than ignoring it. D has no support.

RW2.passage:
Text 1
Some ecologists argue that the return of wolves to Yellowstone National Park in 1995 set off a “trophic cascade.” By hunting elk and making them wary of lingering along streams, wolves reduced the browsing that had stripped willows and aspens, allowing the trees to recover.

Text 2
Other ecologists note that willow recovery in Yellowstone has been patchy, and that elk numbers also fell after 1995 because of human hunting outside the park, drought, and growing populations of bears and cougars. Wolves, they argue, played a role, but the cascade story gives them credit that belongs to several causes at once.
RW2.stem: Based on the texts, how would the ecologists in Text 2 most likely respond to the argument in Text 1?
choices: By denying that wolves had any effect on elk or on the park’s trees
By agreeing that wolves contributed to the decline in browsing while arguing that other factors also reduced elk numbers
By claiming that willows and aspens have fully recovered throughout the park
By arguing that the number of elk in the park increased after wolves returned
RW2.explain: Text 2 grants wolves “played a role” but credits several causes. A overstates their skepticism. C contradicts “patchy.” D contradicts “elk numbers also fell.”

RW2.passage: Field guides long described song as something male songbirds do and females rarely do. Ornithologist Ruth Mbeki surveyed published descriptions of more than 1,000 songbird species and found that females sing in roughly 70 percent of them. Mapping song onto the songbird family tree, she concluded that the common ancestor of today’s songbirds probably had singing females, and that female song was later lost in some lineages, many of them in the temperate regions of Europe and North America where most early ornithologists worked.
RW2.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Mbeki found that female songbirds sing more often than males in most species.
Mbeki’s research suggests that female song is widespread and ancient among songbirds, and that its supposed rarity may reflect where early researchers happened to study birds.
Mbeki concluded that female song evolved recently in temperate songbird species.
Mbeki argues that early ornithologists deliberately ignored female song.
RW2.explain: B combines Mbeki’s two findings (widespread, ancestral) with the implication about temperate-zone bias. A changes “females sing” into “females sing more than males.” C reverses the history: song was lost in some temperate lineages. D adds intent that the text never claims.

They surveyed it in 1948 and drew it in, and then the money went somewhere else.” He tapped a cluster of small squares beside the line. “And this town grew up waiting for it. A gas station, a diner, a motel. Thirty years of people betting on a road that only ever existed here,” he said, and tapped the paper again.

choices: A road completed in 1948 brought travelers through the area.
Mr. Haldane chose the site while surveying the road.

People expected a planned road that was never built to pass beside it.
RW2.explain: The town “grew up waiting for” the road, a road that “was never built” and “only ever existed here” on the map. A contradicts “never built.” C misreads “the money went somewhere else.” Nothing says Mr. Haldane chose the site (B).

RW2.passage: Psychologist Tomoko Sato claims that people remember written information better when it is printed in a hard-to-read font, because the difficulty makes them process the text more carefully.
RW2.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Sato’s claim?
choices: Participants spent more time reading passages printed in a hard-to-read font than passages printed in a clear font.
Students who studied from handouts printed in a hard-to-read font scored higher on a later quiz than students who studied from clear handouts.
In a study with 1,200 participants, recall was no better for text printed in a hard-to-read font than for text in a clear font, even though participants read the hard-to-read text more slowly.
Most participants said they preferred reading text printed in a clear font.
RW2.explain: C shows the slower, more effortful reading happened, yet memory didn’t improve, which breaks the claimed link. A fits Sato’s mechanism. B supports her claim directly. D is about preference, not memory.

RW2.passage: On one of the Galápagos Islands, a severe drought killed most of the plants that produce small, soft seeds, leaving mainly plants with large, hard seeds. In the generation of medium ground finches hatched after the drought, average beak depth was greater than before. Years later, a series of wet seasons brought back the plants with small seeds, and over the following generations average beak depth in the population declined. These observations suggest that
RW2.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

the average beak depth of the population shifts with the kinds of seeds that are available.
medium ground finches prefer small, soft seeds to large, hard ones.
the drought killed mainly the finches with the deepest beaks.
RW2.explain: Beak depth rose after the drought favored big, hard seeds and fell when small seeds returned, so the population tracks the food supply. A is the trap: the changes appear across generations, in a population average, not in individual birds’ beaks. C isn’t addressed. D reverses the result (deeper beaks became more common).

RW2.passage: After a city lowered the speed limit on its residential streets from 30 to 20 miles per hour, crashes on those streets fell by 25 percent over the next two years. During the same two years, however, crashes on the city’s main roads, where the speed limit did not change, fell by about 20 percent. These findings suggest that
RW2.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices: lowering the speed limit had no effect on crashes on residential streets.
main roads became less safe than residential streets during the two years.
much of the decline in crashes on residential streets may have resulted from something other than the lower speed limit.
the city should lower the speed limit on its main roads as well.
RW2.explain: Crashes fell nearly as much on roads without a new limit, so a citywide factor probably drove most of the drop on residential streets too; the limit’s own effect may be small. A goes too far: a 25% vs 20% gap leaves room for some effect. B isn’t supported. D is a recommendation, not an inference from these numbers.

RW2.passage: Electric bicycles cost considerably more to buy than conventional bicycles.  commuters who use them in place of a car often recover the added cost within two years through savings on fuel and parking.

In other words,
Even so,

Consequently,
